weeks.title: State Management at Scale, Beyond useState
weeks.context:
useState works for local component state. When that state needs to be shared across components that are not in a parent-child relationship, props drilling becomes painful: passing state down through three or four layers of components that do not use it themselves, only to pass it further down. State management libraries solve this by providing a store that any component can read from and write to directly.

Zustand is the lightweight state management solution that has largely replaced Redux for new React applications. Where Redux requires actions, reducers, and middleware, Zustand gives you a store in a single function call: useStore(create((set) => ({ count: 0, increment: () => set(state => ({ count: state.count + 1 })) }))). The store is a global singleton. Any component can call useStore(state => state.count) to read the count or useStore(state => state.increment)() to update it, without any Provider wrapping or action dispatching.

The Kanban board you build this week is a complete state management exercise. Board state (columns and their cards) lives in a Zustand store. Multiple components read from and write to the store simultaneously: the column component reads its own cards, the add-card button writes a new card, the drag-and-drop handler updates card positions across columns. No props drilling. Each component takes exactly the slice of state it needs.

Drag and drop is the feature that makes this project feel real. HTML5's native drag-and-drop API handles the browser mechanics. Your job is the state management: when a card is dragged from column A and dropped on column B, you update the store to move the card between columns' card arrays. The immutability requirement means creating new arrays rather than mutating existing ones.

Persistence to localStorage is the layer that makes the data survive page refreshes. Zustand's persist middleware handles this: it subscribes to store updates and writes the state to localStorage on every change. On page load, it rehydrates the store from localStorage before the first render. This one line of middleware gives you persistent state without building any storage logic yourself.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## When useState isn't enough
`useState` handles a component's *local* state beautifully, and lifting state up (W5) shares it with nearby components. But this breaks down when state must be shared across components that are *far apart* in the tree, not in a simple parent-child relationship. The pain is **prop drilling**: passing state down through three or four layers of components that *do not use it themselves*, only to pass it further down to the one that does. Threading a `user` or a `theme` or a `cart` through every intermediate component is tedious, error-prone, and clutters components with props they do not care about. This week you learn the tools that solve this, and, more importantly, the *judgement* of which kind of state-management approach fits which *kind* of state, because the biggest insight of the week is that "state" is not one thing.

## The key insight: state comes in categories
The most important idea this week, which most beginners miss and which prevents enormous confusion, is that **there are different *categories* of state, each with a different best tool**, and using one tool for all of them (the common mistake) leads to pain. The main categories:
- **Server state:** data that lives on the server (fetched from an API/database), the user's posts, the product list, the menu. It is *cached* on the client and can become stale. Tool: a data-fetching library like **TanStack Query**.
- **Global client state:** UI state shared app-wide that is *not* from the server, the theme, a sidebar's open/closed, the current user's session info. Tool: a lightweight store like **Zustand**.
- **URL state:** state that belongs in the URL, the current search query, filters, the page number, the active tab. Tool: the URL itself (search params).
- **Form state:** the values and validation of a form being filled out. Tool: a form library like React Hook Form.
- **Local state:** state used by one component. Tool: `useState` (you already have this).
Recognising *which category* a piece of state is, is the skill that determines which tool to reach for.

## Why categorising state is the whole game
Understanding that state has categories, and matching each to its right tool, is the difference between a clean, maintainable app and a tangled one, which is why this framing leads the week. The classic mistake is treating *all* state the same, typically cramming everything (including server data and URL state) into one global store or into component `useState` with heavy prop-drilling, which produces real problems: server data manually fetched and stored in global state gets stale and requires hand-written caching, loading, and error logic (reinventing, badly, what TanStack Query gives you); filter/search state kept in component state instead of the URL means the page is not shareable or bookmarkable and breaks the back button; global state stuffed with things that should be local makes the app hard to reason about. By contrast, when you put *each* kind of state where it belongs, server data in a query library that handles caching/staleness, global UI state in a simple store, URL state in the URL, form state in a form library, local state in `useState`, each tool does what it is designed for, and the whole app becomes simpler and more correct. So this week is less about learning five libraries and more about developing the *judgement* to recognise a piece of state's category and reach for the matching tool, which is a genuinely senior frontend skill. The tools are easy; knowing which to use is the value.

## Where this fits
This week completes the Frontend phase with state management at scale: the categories of state (server, global, URL, form, local) and the right tool for each (TanStack Query, Zustand, the URL, form libraries, `useState`), the architectural judgement that keeps growing apps clean. It builds on React's state (W5) and completes the frontend stack before the Backend phase (W9-12) turns to the server. Today's orientation: state comes in distinct categories, each with a best-fit tool, and the core skill is recognising which category a piece of state is and managing it accordingly, rather than forcing everything into one approach. Tomorrow you dig into the categories.

items.title: Categories of state
items.body:
## The categories of state, in depth
Today you go deeper on *recognising* each category, because correct categorisation is the whole skill. Ask of any piece of state: *where does it really belong?*
- **Server state** (the big one beginners mishandle): is this data that *lives on the server* and you are showing a *copy* of it? The menu, the user's orders, a list of products, anything fetched from an API. The defining trait: it can become **stale** (the server's copy changes), so it needs *caching, refetching, and synchronisation*, not just storage. It is fundamentally different from client state because *you do not own it*, you are caching a remote source of truth.
- **Global client state:** is this UI state, *owned by the client*, that many components share? The theme, whether a modal is open, the sidebar state, ephemeral app-wide UI. It is yours, it does not come from a server, and it does not become "stale", it just needs to be readable/writable from anywhere.
- **URL state:** does this state describe *what the user is looking at* in a way that should be shareable and bookmarkable? Search terms, filters, sort order, pagination, the active tab. If someone copies the URL, should they see the same view? Then it belongs in the URL.
- **Form state:** the in-progress values and validation of a form.
- **Local state:** used by exactly one component (a dropdown's open/closed, a hover state). `useState` is perfect.

## Why server state is the crucial distinction
The single most valuable categorisation to internalise is **server state vs client state**, because conflating them is the most common and most painful mistake. The instinct of a beginner is to treat fetched server data like any other state: fetch it in a `useEffect`, store it in `useState` (or a global store), and manage loading/error flags by hand. This *works* but reinvents, poorly, a whole set of hard problems that server data has and client state does not: *caching* (don't refetch what you already have), *staleness* (the server's data changed, yours is now wrong), *refetching* (when should you get fresh data? on focus? on interval?), *deduplication* (two components want the same data, fetch once), *loading and error states* (handled consistently), and *optimistic updates*. Server state is genuinely different because it is a *cached copy of a remote source of truth that drifts out of date*, and managing that drift is exactly what dedicated tools (TanStack Query, tomorrow) are built for. Recognising "this is server state, so it needs a server-state tool, not `useState`" is the realisation that eliminates a huge amount of buggy, hand-rolled fetching-and-caching code. Most "my data is stale / I'm fetching the same thing five times / my loading states are a mess" problems are *server state being managed as if it were client state*, and the fix is categorising correctly.

## The discipline: identify the category first
The practical workflow this insight produces is to **identify a piece of state's category *before* choosing how to manage it**, which is a small habit with large payoff. When you have some state, pause and ask: Is it from the server (-> query library)? Is it global client UI (-> store)? Does it belong in the URL (-> search params)? Is it a form (-> form library)? Is it local to one component (-> `useState`)? Answering that *first* tells you the right tool, and prevents the default mistakes (everything in global state, server data in `useState`, filters not in the URL). This categorisation discipline keeps an app's state architecture clean as it grows, because each kind of state lives where it should and is managed by the tool designed for it, rather than everything accreting into one overstuffed global store or scattered ad-hoc fetching. It is the same "match the tool to the problem" judgement that runs through every track, applied to the specific and frequently-muddled domain of frontend state. The libraries you learn this week (TanStack Query, Zustand, etc.) are each *easy*; the skill that makes you effective is the categorisation that tells you when to use which. Master the categories, and state management stops being the confusing mess it is for most developers and becomes a series of clear, right-tool-for-the-job decisions.

## Where this fits
You can categorise state, server (cached remote data that goes stale), global client (shared UI state you own), URL (shareable/bookmarkable view state), form, and local, with server-vs-client as the crucial distinction, and you have the discipline to identify the category *first* and then pick the matching tool. Tomorrow you learn the tool for the most-mishandled category: TanStack Query for server state.

items.title: URL state
items.body:
## URL state: the address bar is state
Some state belongs not in React at all, but in the **URL**. Search queries, filters, sort order, pagination, the active tab, anything that describes *what the user is currently viewing*, should live in the URL's **search params** (`?category=cold&sort=price`), because the URL is shared, bookmarkable, and tied to the browser's history. Instead of `useState` for the active filter, you read and write it from the URL:
```jsx
// Next.js: read and update URL search params
const searchParams = useSearchParams();
const category = searchParams.get('category') ?? 'all';   // state FROM the URL
// to change it, navigate to a new URL with the updated param
router.push(`?category=${newCategory}`);
```
Now the filter is *in the URL*: `/menu?category=cold` shows cold drinks, and that URL captures the view.

## Why these things belong in the URL
The reason filters, search, and pagination belong in the URL rather than component state is a set of concrete, important UX properties that you *lose* if you keep them in `useState`:
- **Shareable:** a user can copy the URL (`/menu?category=cold&sort=price`) and send it, and the recipient sees the *exact same view*. With the state in `useState`, the URL is just `/menu` and the filtered view cannot be shared, a real loss for any filterable/searchable interface.
- **Bookmarkable:** the user can bookmark the filtered/searched view and return to it. `useState` state is gone on reload; URL state persists.
- **Back/forward works:** because the state is in the URL, the browser's back button correctly returns to the previous filter/page, and forward works too. With `useState`, the back button does *not* undo a filter change (it leaves the page entirely), which violates user expectations, a classic bug where "back" does the wrong thing because the view state was not in the URL.
- **Refresh-safe:** reloading the page keeps the view (the URL still has the params), where `useState` resets to default on reload.
These properties, shareable, bookmarkable, back-button-correct, refresh-safe, are exactly what users expect from search and filters, and the *only* way to get them is to put that state in the URL. So the rule is firm: **if state describes a shareable/navigable view, it belongs in the URL.**

## The principle: the URL is part of your app's state
The deeper idea is that **the URL is a legitimate, important place to store state**, not just an address, and treating it as such is a mark of thoughtful frontend architecture. Many developers default to `useState` for *everything* about the current view, and then bolt on hacks when users complain that sharing a link does not work or the back button is broken, whereas the right design is to recognise from the start that view-describing state (what is searched, filtered, sorted, paged, selected) *is* URL state and put it there. This has a nice consequence: the URL becomes a *complete description* of what the user is looking at, so the app's view is fully determined by the URL (plus the server data), which is clean, predictable, and gives you all the shareable/bookmarkable/navigable behaviour for free from the browser. It also composes with the rest: server state (TanStack Query) often *depends* on URL state (the search query in the URL drives the query that fetches results), a natural and powerful pairing where the URL holds *what* to show and TanStack Query fetches it. Recognising URL state as a category, and deliberately putting view-state in the URL rather than reflexively in `useState`, is a specific, high-value piece of the state-categorisation judgement, and it directly produces the shareable, navigable, back-button-correct behaviour that distinguishes a polished app from a frustrating one. The address bar is state; use it.

## Where this fits
You understand URL state: view-describing state (search, filters, sort, pagination, active tab) belongs in the URL's search params, which makes it shareable, bookmarkable, back-button-correct, and refresh-safe, properties `useState` cannot give, and the URL becomes a complete description of the current view, pairing naturally with server-state fetching. Tomorrow you handle the form-state category with a dedicated form library.

items.title: Form state
items.body:
## Form state: a dedicated tool for a common need Forms are everywhere and have their own kind of state, the field values, validation errors, touched/dirty status, submission state, and managing all that with raw `useState` (a piece of state and an onChange per field, plus manual validation) gets verbose and error-prone for anything beyond a trivial form. **React Hook Form** (the standard) is the dedicated tool, handling form state efficiently with minimal boilerplate: ```jsx const { register, handleSubmit, formState: { errors } } = useForm(); function onSubmit(data) { /* data = all field values, already collected */ } return (
{errors.email && {errors.email.message}}
); ``` `register` wires each input into the form's state, `handleSubmit` collects all the values and runs your handler, and validation rules (and their error messages) are declared inline, all the form plumbing, handled. ## What a form library handles for you A form library earns its place by handling the genuinely-tedious parts of forms that raw `useState` makes you write by hand: - **Field registration and values:** `register` connects inputs to the form state, so you do not write a `useState` + `onChange` per field, the library tracks all values. - **Validation:** declare rules per field (required, format, min/max, custom), and get error messages and validity, instead of hand-writing validation logic and error state. It integrates with schema validators (like Zod) for typed, reusable validation shared with the backend. - **Submission handling:** `handleSubmit` collects values, runs validation, and calls your handler only with valid data, handling the prevent-default and value-gathering for you. - **Field state:** which fields are touched, dirty, or in error, so you can show errors only after a field is touched, disable submit until valid, etc. - **Performance:** React Hook Form is optimised to minimise re-renders (it uses uncontrolled inputs under the hood with refs), so large forms stay fast where many controlled `useState` fields would re-render heavily. For any non-trivial form, this is a large reduction in code *and* an increase in correctness (consistent validation, proper error display), which is why a form library is the standard for real forms. ## When a library, and when raw React is fine The judgement, consistent with the week's theme, is to match the tool to the form's complexity, not reach for the library reflexively *nor* hand-roll a complex form. **Raw `useState` controlled inputs** (W5) are perfectly fine for a *simple* form, one or two fields, minimal validation, where the library would be unnecessary overhead, and it is good that you understand the controlled-component fundamentals the library is built on. **A form library** (React Hook Form) is the right call for *real* forms, multiple fields, meaningful validation, error handling, where its boilerplate reduction and built-in validation/error/submission handling pay off clearly. The signal to reach for it: you find yourself writing repetitive `useState`+`onChange`+validation+error-state code per field, that repetition *is* what the library eliminates. This is the same "use the dedicated tool when the problem warrants it, raw approach when it is simple" judgement as everywhere else, applied to form state. Recognising form state as its own category with a dedicated best-fit tool (for non-trivial cases) completes another piece of the state-categorisation picture: forms are not just "a bunch of useState", they are a distinct concern with a tool designed for it, and using that tool for real forms keeps your form code clean, correct, and consistent. For Bean Forge's simple contact form, controlled `useState` is fine; for a multi-step signup or a complex settings form, React Hook Form is the right tool. ## Where this fits You understand form state as its own category: managed cleanly by a dedicated library (React Hook Form) that handles field registration, validation, errors, submission, and performance with minimal boilerplate, used for real forms while raw controlled `useState` suffices for simple ones. Tomorrow you go deeper on the subtleties of server-state freshness: stale time, cache time, and refetching.

days.title: Stale time, cache time, refetch on focus
days.summary: Focus: Stale time, cache time, refetch on focus

items.title: Stale time, cache time, refetch on focus
items.body:
## Tuning server-state freshness
TanStack Query manages server data's freshness automatically, but *how fresh* and *how often to refetch* are tunable, and understanding the key settings, **stale time**, **cache time**, and **refetch-on-focus**, lets you balance data freshness against unnecessary requests. The core settings:
```jsx
useQuery({
  queryKey: ['menu'],
  queryFn: fetchMenu,
  staleTime: 60_000,          // data is "fresh" for 60s; won't refetch within that
  gcTime: 300_000,            // keep unused cached data for 5 min before discarding
  refetchOnWindowFocus: true, // refetch when the user returns to the tab
});
```
These control the trade-off between always-fresh data (more requests) and fewer requests (possibly slightly stale data), and tuning them appropriately for each kind of data is a real optimisation.

## What each setting does, and the trade-off
Understanding these three settings clarifies how server-state caching actually behaves:
- **`staleTime`** (how long data is considered *fresh*): within the stale time, TanStack Query serves the cached data *without* refetching (it trusts it is current); after the stale time, the data is "stale" and will be refetched in the background on the next trigger (mount, focus). A *longer* stale time means fewer refetches (good for data that rarely changes, a list of countries) but a higher chance of showing slightly out-of-date data; a *shorter* stale time means fresher data but more requests. You set it per the data's volatility: long for stable data, short (or zero) for rapidly-changing data.
- **`gcTime`** (garbage-collection / cache time): how long to keep *unused* cached data (data no component is currently using) before discarding it. A longer cache time means returning to a screen shows instant cached data even after being away a while; shorter frees memory sooner. It is about how long the cache *persists*, distinct from how long data is considered *fresh*.
- **`refetchOnWindowFocus`** (refetch when the user returns to the tab): on by default, and usually desirable, when a user switches back to your app, refetch potentially-stale data so they see current information. You might disable it for data that does not need such freshness, to avoid extra requests.
The unifying trade-off is **freshness vs request count**: tighter settings keep data more current at the cost of more network requests (and load), looser settings reduce requests at the cost of potential staleness, and the right balance *depends on the data*.

## Matching freshness to the data: the real skill
The practical skill, and the deeper lesson, is **matching the freshness settings to how volatile and how critical each kind of data is**, rather than using one setting for everything. Different server data has different freshness needs: a user's account balance or a live inventory count should be very fresh (short stale time, refetch on focus), because showing stale values there is harmful; a list of blog categories or a product catalog changes rarely, so a long stale time avoids needless refetches with no real downside; a dashboard might refetch on an interval. Using a single global setting ignores this, either over-fetching stable data (wasteful) or under-fetching volatile data (showing stale values). So you *tune per query* based on the data's nature: how often does it really change, and how bad is it to show a slightly old value? This is a nuanced, real-world optimisation that balances user-perceived freshness, network/server load, and cost, and it is the kind of detail that separates a thoughtfully-built data layer from a naive one. It also reflects the broader truth from this whole week: even *within* the server-state category, good management means understanding the specific data and configuring the tool to match it, not applying one setting blindly. TanStack Query gives you sensible defaults (so you need not tune everything), but knowing *what* staleTime, gcTime, and refetch-on-focus do lets you deliberately tune the freshness-vs-requests trade-off where it matters, which is the mark of someone who understands server-state caching rather than just using it. Match the freshness to the data.

## Where this fits
You can tune server-state freshness: `staleTime` (how long data is fresh before refetching), `gcTime` (how long unused cache persists), and `refetchOnWindowFocus`, understanding the freshness-vs-request-count trade-off and the skill of matching it to each data's volatility and criticality. This completes your command of server state. Tomorrow you assemble the week's state-management knowledge and ship.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a well-architected state layer
You assemble the week into an app (or a feature) with a clean, correctly-categorised state architecture, demonstrating the judgement that is the week's real lesson:
- **server state** via TanStack Query (cached, deduplicated, with appropriate freshness settings).
- **global client state** via a lightweight store (Zustand) where state is genuinely shared app-wide.
- **URL state** for filters/search/pagination (shareable, bookmarkable, back-button-correct).
- **form state** via a form library for real forms, and **local state** via `useState` where appropriate.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "State architecture: server (TanStack Query), global (Zustand), URL, form, local - each in its place"
git push
```

## The deliverable is the *architecture*, the right tool per category
What makes this project demonstrate real frontend competence is that *each kind of state is managed by the right tool*, which is a senior-level architectural decision most developers get wrong. The strongest version shows clear, deliberate categorisation: server data is in TanStack Query (not hand-fetched into `useState`), filters and search are in the URL (so views are shareable and the back button works), genuinely-global UI state is in a small store (not prop-drilled through ten components), forms use a form library where warranted, and local state stays local. The proof is in what *works* as a result: data is fresh and not redundantly fetched, filtered views are shareable links, the back button behaves correctly, and the codebase has no prop-drilling tangle or stale-data bugs, all consequences of putting each state in its proper place. Being able to look at a piece of state and *correctly categorise it* (this is server state, this belongs in the URL, this is truly global, this is local) and reach for the matching tool is exactly the judgement that distinguishes a well-architected app from a tangled one, and it is the deliverable. Anyone can use the libraries; using the *right one for each category* is the skill.

## What state management established, and the frontend phase
Step back: you have learned the architecture of frontend state, which is one of the most confusing areas for developers and one where good judgement has outsized impact. The core lesson is *categorisation*: state is not one thing but several kinds, server (TanStack Query, with freshness tuning), global client (a store), URL (the address bar), form (a form library), and local (`useState`), and the skill is recognising which category a piece of state is and managing it with the right tool, rather than forcing everything into one approach. This judgement keeps apps clean as they scale and eliminates whole classes of bugs (stale data, broken back buttons, prop-drilling messes, inconsistent loading states). And it completes the **Frontend phase**: you can now build interfaces (React's component model and declarative state), take them to production (Next.js App Router's server/client architecture), style them beautifully and accessibly (Tailwind, shadcn/Radix, tasteful motion), and architect their state correctly (the right tool per category). That is the complete modern frontend skill set, the one most frontend and full-stack jobs require, and it is FORGE's own stack throughout.

## Where this fits
You shipped an app with a correctly-categorised state architecture (server, global, URL, form, local, each in its proper tool), completing the Frontend phase and the senior judgement of matching state to the right management approach. You now command modern frontend end to end. Next comes the **Backend phase** (W9-12), where you turn to the server side, Node.js and Express, PostgreSQL and Prisma, REST API design, and authentication, building the server, database, and APIs that your frontends consume, which makes you a true *full-stack* developer.

weeks.title: Node.js, Express, and the Server Side of JavaScript
weeks.context:
The browser runs JavaScript. The server is separate, a different process, often on a different machine, that receives HTTP requests and sends responses. Node.js lets you write server-side JavaScript with the same language you use in the browser, but the environment is completely different: no window object, no DOM, no localStorage. Instead, you have access to the filesystem, environment variables, databases, and the ability to listen for incoming HTTP requests.

Express is the minimal web framework for Node.js. Where Next.js is opinionated and full-featured, Express is a thin layer over Node's HTTP server that adds middleware (functions that process requests and responses), routing (mapping URLs to handler functions), and nothing else. Understanding Express means understanding how web servers work at the HTTP level, without framework magic hiding the details.

The URL shortener you build has one real engineering challenge: generating short codes. A 7-character alphanumeric code from a 62-character alphabet (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) gives 62^7 = 3.5 trillion possibilities, more than enough. But the codes must be unique. The two approaches are random generation with collision checking (generate a code, check if it exists in the database, retry if it does) and counter-based encoding (encode the auto-incrementing row ID as base62). The counter approach is simpler and has no collision risk.

TypeScript on the server is the same TypeScript you use in the browser, the same type system, the same compiler, but the types describe server-specific things: request bodies, response schemas, database row types. Defining these types explicitly catches entire categories of bugs before they reach production. A handler that expects req.body.url to be a string and receives undefined instead will throw a runtime error. A TypeScript type catching that discrepancy catches it at compile time.

The redirect endpoint is the product. When someone visits your short URL (e.g., short.ly/abc1234), your server looks up the code in the database, increments the click count, and responds with an HTTP 301 redirect to the original URL. The browser follows the redirect transparently. The entire user experience is seamless, they just end up at the destination.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Crossing to the server side
Everything so far ran in the browser (or, with Next.js, partly on a server the framework managed). This week you cross fully to the **server side** and understand it directly. The server is a *separate process*, often on a different machine, that receives HTTP requests and sends responses, and **Node.js** lets you write that server in JavaScript, the same language you already know. But the *environment* is completely different from the browser: there is no `window`, no DOM, no `localStorage`, instead you have the filesystem, environment variables, databases, and the ability to *listen for incoming HTTP requests*. You learn Node and **Express** (the minimal server framework) this week, gaining the server-side foundation that, combined with your frontend skills, makes you a true *full-stack* developer.

## Node.js: JavaScript outside the browser
The key realisation about **Node.js** is that it is JavaScript running *outside the browser*, in a different environment with different capabilities. The *language* is identical (variables, functions, async, the same JavaScript), but the *environment* is the opposite of the browser's:
```text
BROWSER environment:        window, document (DOM), localStorage, fetch, no filesystem
NODE (server) environment:  filesystem, env vars, databases, listen for HTTP requests,
                            NO window, NO DOM, NO localStorage
```
This makes sense once you see *why*: the browser's job is rendering a page for a user, so it has the DOM and storage but is sandboxed away from the machine; the server's job is handling requests and data, so it has filesystem and database access but no concept of a "page" or a "window." Same language, different powers suited to different jobs. Knowing JavaScript already means you do not learn a new language for the backend, you learn a new *environment* and its capabilities, which is a much smaller leap and one of the great advantages of full-stack JavaScript: one language, both sides.

## Express: a thin, honest web framework
**Express** is the minimal web framework for Node, and learning it (rather than only a heavy framework) is deliberate, because it teaches how web servers *actually work* at the HTTP level. Where Next.js is opinionated and full-featured (it does a lot for you, sometimes magically), Express is a *thin layer* over Node's built-in HTTP server that adds two things and little else: **routing** (mapping URLs to handler functions) and **middleware** (functions that process requests/responses in a chain), and *nothing else*. This minimalism is the point: with Express, *you* assemble the server from clear, explicit pieces, so you see exactly how a request comes in, flows through middleware, hits a route handler, and produces a response, with no framework magic hiding it. Understanding Express means understanding the HTTP request/response cycle (which you have met since week 1) from the *server's* side, concretely, which is foundational knowledge that transfers to *every* backend framework (Next.js route handlers, and the backends in other languages all work the same way). You learn the un-abstracted server, so the abstracted ones make sense.

## Where this fits
This opens the **Backend phase** (W9-12): Node and Express (the server, this week), PostgreSQL and Prisma (the database, W10), REST API design (W11), and authentication (W12), the server side that your frontends consume, making you full-stack. It builds on the HTTP fundamentals from week 1 and the route-handler glimpse from Next.js (W6), now as direct server-side work. Today's orientation: the server is a separate process; Node.js is JavaScript in a server environment (filesystem, databases, listening for requests, no DOM); and Express is a minimal framework (routing + middleware) that reveals how web servers work at the HTTP level. Tomorrow you dig into the Node.js runtime.

items.title: The Node.js runtime
items.body:
## How Node actually runs your code
To use Node well, understand its **runtime** model, which is distinctive and explains both its strengths and its quirks. Node is **single-threaded** with an **event loop** and **non-blocking I/O**, a combination that sounds technical but is the key to how it handles many requests efficiently:
```text
Node: ONE main thread runs your JavaScript, with an EVENT LOOP.
  - I/O operations (reading a file, querying a database, a network call) are NON-BLOCKING:
    Node starts them and CONTINUES, handling other work, then runs your callback when they finish.
  - so one thread juggles thousands of concurrent requests by never sitting idle waiting on I/O.
```
This is the same event-driven idea you met in the browser (register a handler, react when the event fires), now as the *core execution model* of the whole runtime. Node does not wait around for a slow database query, it kicks off the query and goes to handle other requests, running your code to handle the result when the query completes.

## Why non-blocking I/O matters for a server
Understanding *why* Node is built this way explains what it is good at (and not). A web server's work is overwhelmingly **I/O-bound**: a typical request reads from a database, calls another service, or reads a file, then waits for those (relatively slow) operations to return, the server spends most of its time *waiting on I/O*, not computing. Node's non-blocking model is ideal for this: while one request is waiting on its database query, the single thread is free to start handling other requests, so one Node process can juggle thousands of concurrent connections efficiently, because it is never blocked idle waiting, it is always doing useful work for *some* request while others wait on their I/O. This is why Node became so popular for web servers and APIs: web work is mostly waiting on I/O, and Node's event loop turns that waiting time into capacity for other requests. The flip side, and the limit to know, is that Node's single thread is *not* ideal for **CPU-bound** work (heavy computation, image processing, large calculations): a long synchronous computation *blocks* the single thread, freezing all other requests until it finishes, the dreaded "blocking the event loop." So Node excels at I/O-heavy web servers (most web apps) and struggles with CPU-heavy tasks (which you offload to other processes/workers). Knowing this, Node is great for the I/O-bound work of typical web servers, weak for CPU-bound work, tells you both why it fits web development and when to reach for something else.

## The practical consequence: don't block the loop
The single most important practical rule the runtime model implies is **never block the event loop**, because Node's whole efficiency depends on the single thread staying free to handle other requests. This means: always use the *asynchronous*, non-blocking versions of operations (async file reads, async database queries, never the synchronous ones in request handling), and avoid long synchronous computations in your request path (a heavy `for` loop crunching numbers blocks *every* other request while it runs). The symptom of violating this is a server that becomes unresponsive under load even though it is not "busy" in the usual sense, one blocking operation has frozen the single thread. This is why the next lesson (async patterns) is so central: in Node, asynchronous programming is not an occasional technique, it is *the* way you handle the I/O that is most of a server's work, precisely so the event loop stays unblocked. Understanding the runtime, single thread, event loop, non-blocking I/O, and the rule never to block it, is the foundation for writing Node servers that handle real concurrent load, and it explains *why* Node code is so heavily asynchronous (it has to be, to keep the one thread free). Internalising "one thread, keep it unblocked, do I/O asynchronously" is the key to Node.

## Where this fits
You understand the Node runtime: single-threaded with an event loop and non-blocking I/O, which makes it excellent for the I/O-bound work of web servers (juggling many concurrent requests by never idling on I/O) but poor for CPU-bound work, with the critical rule to never block the event loop. This is why Node code is heavily asynchronous, which you handle next. Tomorrow you meet Node's standard library, the server-side capabilities you now have.

items.title: The standard library
items.body:
## Node's standard library: your server-side powers
Now that you are on the server, you have a whole set of capabilities the browser lacked, and Node's **standard library** (built-in modules) provides them. The ones you reach for most:
```js
import fs from 'node:fs/promises';     // filesystem: read/write files
import path from 'node:path';          // work with file paths correctly across OSes
import http from 'node:http';          // the HTTP server (Express wraps this)
import crypto from 'node:crypto';      // hashing, random tokens, security primitives
import process from 'node:process';    // env vars, the running process, exit
// also: os, url, stream, events, and more
```
And `process.env` gives you **environment variables**, how you read configuration and secrets (database URLs, API keys) on the server:
```js
const dbUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL;   // a secret, set in the environment, never in code
```
These built-ins are your server-side toolkit, the filesystem, HTTP, crypto, process/env access that the browser deliberately denied a web page but a server needs.

## Environment variables and secrets: a foundational discipline
The most important standard-library concept for real-world backends is **environment variables for configuration and secrets**, because it is foundational to building software securely and correctly. A server needs configuration (which database to connect to, which port to listen on) and *secrets* (database passwords, API keys, signing secrets), and these must *not* be hard-coded in your source code, because code goes into git (and often public repos), and a secret in git is a leaked secret. Instead, you read them from the *environment* (`process.env.DATABASE_URL`), and you *set* them outside the code, in a `.env` file locally (which is git-ignored, never committed) and in your hosting platform's settings in production. This separation, **configuration and secrets live in the environment, not the code**, has several payoffs: secrets stay out of source control (security), the *same* code runs in different environments (local, staging, production) just by changing the env vars (the database URL differs per environment but the code is identical), and you can rotate a secret without touching code. This is a non-negotiable discipline, you saw it referenced in the AI-eng deployment work (API keys as managed secrets), and now you implement it on the server: never commit secrets, always read config from `process.env`, keep a git-ignored `.env` locally, and set the real values in the platform for production. Getting this right from the start is foundational security hygiene, and getting it wrong (a hard-coded password, a committed `.env`) is one of the most common and damaging beginner mistakes.

## Modules and the npm ecosystem
The standard library also frames how Node code is *organised* and *extended*, which is worth grounding. Node uses **modules**: you split code into files that `export` functionality and `import` it where needed (the same import/export you used in frontend), so a server is composed of focused modules (a route module, a database module, a utils module) rather than one giant file, the same component-thinking, applied to backend code organisation. And beyond the standard library, the vast **npm ecosystem** (the same `npm` from the frontend) gives you packages for everything (Express itself is an npm package, plus libraries for auth, validation, database access, and more), so you build on a huge body of existing code rather than writing everything from scratch. The judgement, familiar from across the track, is to use the standard library for what it covers (filesystem, crypto, HTTP basics) and reach for well-chosen npm packages for higher-level needs (a web framework like Express, an ORM like Prisma), while being thoughtful about dependencies (each one is code you rely on and must trust/maintain). Understanding that a Node server is *modules* (your organised code) plus the *standard library* (built-in capabilities) plus *npm packages* (the ecosystem) gives you the full picture of how server-side JavaScript projects are built, and the environment-variable discipline gives you the foundational security hygiene that real backends require.

## Where this fits
You know Node's standard library (filesystem, HTTP, crypto, process/env) and, crucially, the environment-variable discipline for configuration and secrets (read from `process.env`, never hard-code, git-ignore `.env`, set real values in the platform), plus how Node code is organised into modules and extended via npm. Tomorrow you handle the async patterns that Node's I/O-heavy, never-block-the-loop nature demands.

items.title: Process management
items.body:
## Running the server: process management
A server is a *long-running process*, it starts and stays running, listening for requests, unlike a script that runs and exits, and **process management** is about running, configuring, and keeping that process alive reliably. The core concerns:
- **Starting and listening:** your server starts and *listens* on a port for incoming requests (`app.listen(process.env.PORT || 3000)`), staying alive to handle them.
- **Configuration via environment:** the process reads its config (port, database URL, secrets) from environment variables (D3), so the *same* process runs differently in different environments.
- **Keeping it running:** in production, the process must be kept alive, restarted if it crashes, and managed (a process manager like PM2, or the hosting platform's process supervision, restarts a crashed process so the server recovers).
- **Graceful shutdown:** when the process is told to stop (a deploy, a restart), it should finish in-flight requests and close database connections cleanly, rather than dropping requests, so users are not affected by a restart.
- **Logging:** the process should log what it does (requests, errors) so you can see what is happening in production (the observability foundation, W20).

## Why process thinking matters for the backend
The shift to think about your server as a *managed, long-running process* is important because it is fundamentally different from frontend code and from one-off scripts, and getting the process concerns right is what makes a server *production-ready* rather than just functional on your laptop. A frontend runs in each user's browser (the user "manages" it by opening a tab); a server is *one* process (or several) that *you* run and must keep alive, serving *all* users, so its uptime, recovery, and clean lifecycle are your responsibility. This reframes several things: the server *will* eventually crash (a bug, an unhandled error, a dependency failure), so it must be *supervised* to restart automatically, or an unrecovered crash means downtime for everyone; deploys *restart* the process, so graceful shutdown (don't drop in-flight requests) matters for a smooth deploy; and configuration must come from the environment so the one codebase runs correctly across environments. These process concerns, start, listen, configure from env, supervise/restart, shut down gracefully, log, are the operational reality of running a backend, and they connect forward to the deployment, scaling, and observability weeks (W19-22) where they become central. Thinking of the server as a process you operate (not just code you write) is the mindset that distinguishes backend engineering from frontend coding.

## Keep it operationally simple, lean on the platform
The practical guidance, consistent with the track, is that you do *not* need to hand-build all of this, modern hosting platforms (the Node equivalents of the Netlify/Vercel you have used) handle much of the process management for you, supervising and restarting your process, managing environment variables, capturing logs, so you focus on the application while the platform handles keeping it alive. So for most projects you *write* the server (with sensible startup, env-based config, graceful shutdown, and logging) and *deploy* it to a platform that supervises the process, rather than running and babysitting raw processes yourself. The skills to build *in* are the ones that make your process play well with that management: read config from env (so the platform can configure it), handle errors so the process does not crash unnecessarily, shut down gracefully on the stop signal (so deploys are clean), and log usefully (so the platform's log capture is meaningful). Understanding process management, even while leaning on the platform for the heavy lifting, is what lets you build and deploy a server that runs reliably for real users, recovering from crashes, surviving deploys, configured correctly per environment, which is the operational competence that turns a server that works on your machine into one that works in production. The same start-simple, lean-on-the-platform judgement from earlier deployment work applies: understand the concerns, implement the parts that are yours, and let the platform manage the rest.

## Where this fits
You understand process management: running the server as a long-running, environment-configured, supervised, gracefully-shutdown, logging process, the operational reality of a backend, while leaning on hosting platforms for the heavy lifting (supervision, env, logs) and building in the parts that make your process manageable. Tomorrow you survey the alternatives to Node, to place it among the backend options.

items.title: Alternatives
items.body:
## Node among the alternatives
You have learned Node because it lets you write the backend in JavaScript (one language, full-stack), but it is one of many backend choices, and understanding the **alternatives** lets you place Node honestly and choose deliberately. The major server-side options, at a glance:
- **Node.js (JavaScript/TypeScript):** same language as the frontend (full-stack JS), huge ecosystem (npm), great for I/O-bound web servers, the strengths you have seen. Weaker for CPU-heavy work.
- **Python** (Django, FastAPI, Flask): hugely popular, especially where the backend touches data/ML (the ML and AI tracks live here), very readable, strong ecosystem.
- **Go:** compiled, fast, excellent concurrency (built for it), great for high-performance services and infrastructure, more verbose, less batteries-included.
- **Ruby** (Rails), **Java/Kotlin** (Spring), **C#** (.NET), **Rust**, and others, each with strengths and niches.
And within the Node world, there are alternatives to Express itself (Fastify for performance, NestJS for structure, plus the newer runtimes Deno and Bun that run JavaScript with modern improvements).

## How to think about choosing a backend
The point of surveying alternatives is to make backend choice a *deliberate, context-driven decision* rather than dogma, and the factors that actually matter are practical:
- **Team and ecosystem:** what does your team know, and what libraries/community support exist for your domain? A Python shop, or a project heavy in data/ML, leans Python; a JavaScript team building a web app leans Node (one language across the stack is a real advantage).
- **The workload:** I/O-bound web APIs (most web apps) suit Node, Python, Ruby well; CPU-heavy or high-concurrency, performance-critical services suit Go, Rust, Java better. Match the runtime to the work (the same I/O-vs-CPU distinction from D2).
- **Full-stack synergy:** Node's standout advantage is *one language for frontend and backend*, sharing code, types (TypeScript), and mental model across the stack, which is a genuine productivity and consistency win for full-stack JavaScript teams, and a big reason Node is so common for web apps.
- **Existing constraints:** what the rest of the system uses, what the company has standardised on, what you are integrating with.
There is no single "best" backend, only the one that fits your team, workload, and context, exactly the match-the-tool-to-the-problem judgement that recurs across every track. Knowing the landscape lets you make that call (and understand systems built in other languages) rather than assuming the one you learned is universally right.

## Why this perspective matters
The deeper value of knowing the alternatives is intellectual honesty and adaptability: you learned Node, and Node is an excellent, popular choice *for web servers*, but it is *a* choice with specific strengths (full-stack JS, I/O-bound web work, huge ecosystem) and weaknesses (CPU-bound work), not a universal answer. Recognising this keeps you from the beginner trap of thinking "the tech I learned is the right tech for everything," and prepares you to work in, or evaluate, backends written in other languages (you will encounter Python backends right next door in the ML/AI tracks, Go services in infrastructure, and so on). It also means that *what you learned this week is transferable*: the concepts, the HTTP request/response cycle, routing and middleware, async I/O, environment-based config, process management, REST APIs (next week), authentication, are *universal* to backend development, the *same* across Node, Python, Go, and the rest, just expressed in different syntax. So the durable takeaway is that you have learned *backend engineering* (the concepts), using Node as the vehicle, and those concepts carry to any backend, while Node specifically is the right tool when full-stack JavaScript and I/O-bound web work fit, which is a great many web projects. This perspective, Node is an excellent choice among several, the concepts transfer everywhere, choose deliberately by context, is what makes you a backend engineer rather than just a Node programmer.

## Where this fits
You can place Node among the backend alternatives (Python, Go, and others), choosing deliberately by team, ecosystem, workload (I/O vs CPU), and full-stack synergy, and you recognise that the *concepts* you learned (HTTP, routing/middleware, async, config, process, REST, auth) are universal across backends while Node is the right vehicle when full-stack JS and web work fit. Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship a Node/Express server.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a Node/Express server
You assemble the week into a working Express server, your first standalone backend, demonstrating the server-side fundamentals:
- an **Express** app with **routes** (URLs mapped to handlers) and **middleware** (request processing), serving real HTTP endpoints.
- proper **async/await** with error handling for any I/O, **environment-based** configuration and secrets (no hard-coded values), and a server that **listens** and runs as a managed process.
- clean **module** organisation, and the server deployed to a Node-hosting platform.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Express server: routes, middleware, async, env config - the server side"
git push   # deploy to a Node host (Railway, Render, Fly, etc.)
```

## The deliverable: a real server you understand
What makes this project show real backend competence is that you built a server *from explicit pieces you understand*, not framework magic. The strongest version shows clean routing (URLs to handlers), middleware doing real work (logging, parsing, error handling) in an explicit chain, async I/O with proper error handling, and environment-based config with secrets kept out of code, all the fundamentals of how a web server actually works, assembled by you. The proof is that you can *explain the request lifecycle*: a request comes in, flows through the middleware chain, hits the matching route handler, which does async work (e.g. a database query) with error handling, and returns a response, the HTTP cycle from the *server's* side, demystified. Because Express is minimal, this understanding is explicit (nothing is hidden), which is exactly why learning it teaches the universal backend model that transfers to every framework. Demonstrating that you understand how a web server works at the HTTP level, routing, middleware, async I/O, config, the request lifecycle, rather than just calling a framework's magic, is the deliverable, and it is the foundation everything else in the backend phase builds on.

## What Node and Express established
Step back: you have crossed to the server side and gained the backend foundation. You understand the server as a separate process; Node as JavaScript in a server environment (filesystem, databases, no DOM) with a single-threaded, non-blocking, event-loop runtime suited to I/O-bound web work; Express as the minimal routing-and-middleware framework that reveals the HTTP request/response cycle from the server's side; the pervasive async/await with error handling that Node's model demands; environment-based configuration and secrets; process management; and Node's place among the alternatives. Crucially, you learned the *un-abstracted* server (minimal Express, explicit pieces), so the abstracted ones (Next.js route handlers, and other frameworks) make sense, and the *concepts* you gained are universal backend engineering that transfers to any language. Combined with your frontend skills, you are now genuinely *full-stack*: you can build both the client and the server. The server you built is the thing your frontends consume, completing the two-sided picture of web development.

## Where this fits
You shipped a Node/Express server and understand backend development from the HTTP level up, the server side that makes you full-stack. A server needs data, though, and that data needs to be stored properly. Next week you build the data layer: **PostgreSQL** (the production database), **Prisma** (the type-safe ORM and migration system), and the skill of *designing data you won't regret*, schemas, indexes, and migrations, so your backend has a robust, well-structured foundation for the information it manages.

items.body: Your Express route POST /shorten receives a JSON body with a url field. You call req.body.url without any validation. What risks does this create and how do you address them? (1) req.body.url might be undefined (request body is malformed or the field is missing), causing a runtime error when you try to use it. (2) It might be a string but not a valid URL (e.g., "javascript:alert('xss')", a protocol that can execute code when used as a redirect target). (3) It might be a very long string that overloads your database. Fix: use Zod or express-validator to parse and validate the request body before using it. Check that url is a string, parse it with new URL(url) to verify it is a valid URL, check the protocol is http or https, and enforce a maximum length.

weeks.title: PostgreSQL, Prisma, and Designing Data You Won't Regret
weeks.context:
SQLite was right for getting started, zero configuration, single file, no server to manage. But it has real limits: no concurrent writes (only one writer at a time), no network access (the database must be on the same machine as the application), and limited tooling for production management. PostgreSQL is the production database that most web applications use. This week you migrate your URL shortener from SQLite to PostgreSQL and add Prisma as the ORM.

Prisma is an ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) that provides three things: a type-safe query client, a schema definition language, and a migration system. The schema (schema.prisma) is the single source of truth for your database structure. Prisma generates TypeScript types from it and generates migration SQL from it. When you add a field, you add it to the schema and Prisma generates the ALTER TABLE migration. You never write migration SQL by hand.

Database design deserves more attention than most beginners give it. The decisions you make now, table names, column types, nullability, foreign key constraints, indexes, are hard to change after the application is running with real data. The URL shortener has two main entities: Url (the link record with short code and original URL) and Click (each redirect event). The relationship is one-to-many: one URL has many clicks. How you model this relationship, what indexes you create, and how you handle deletion cascades all affect query performance and data integrity.

Prisma migrations are the mechanism that applies schema changes to the database safely. In development, prisma migrate dev generates and applies a new migration. In production, prisma migrate deploy applies pending migrations without prompting. The migration history is stored in the prisma/migrations directory and committed to git, this is the database's version history, analogous to git commits for code.

Connection pooling is the production concern that SQLite never required. PostgreSQL connections are expensive, establishing a new connection takes 50-100ms. An application that creates a new connection per request cannot handle significant traffic. Prisma manages a connection pool automatically, reusing connections across requests. The pool size is configurable: too small and requests queue waiting for a connection, too large and you hit PostgreSQL's maximum connections limit.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Data you won't regret
A server needs to *store* data, and where and how you store it has long-lasting consequences, hence the week's title: *designing data you won't regret*. **PostgreSQL** is the production database most web applications use, and this week you move to it (migrating from SQLite, which was fine to start but has real limits) and add **Prisma** as the ORM, the type-safe layer between your code and the database. More than the tools, this week teaches *data modelling*: designing schemas, indexes, and migrations so your data foundation is robust, fast, and able to evolve, because a bad data design is one of the hardest things to fix later (your whole app depends on it), while a good one supports the application for years. This is FORGE's stack too (Postgres + Prisma), so it is directly real-world relevant.

## Why move from SQLite to PostgreSQL
You may have started with SQLite, and it was the right choice for getting going: zero configuration, a single file, no server to manage. But it has real limits that production hits, and understanding them shows *why* you move to Postgres:
- **No concurrent writes:** SQLite allows only *one writer at a time*, which is fine for a single-user or low-traffic situation but a hard bottleneck for a real web app with many simultaneous users writing data.
- **No network access:** the SQLite database must be on the *same machine* as the application (it is a file), which does not fit the typical production setup where the app and database are separate, scalable services.
- **Limited production tooling:** less of the management, monitoring, and scaling tooling that production databases need.
**PostgreSQL** solves all of these: it is a real database *server* (runs as its own process, accessed over the network), handles many concurrent readers *and* writers, and has rich production tooling, which is why it is the default production database for web applications. The migration from SQLite to Postgres is the standard "we're getting serious" step, and knowing *why* (concurrency, network, tooling) is the point, not change for its own sake, but the specific limits SQLite hits that Postgres resolves.

## Prisma: the type-safe data layer
**Prisma** is an **ORM** (Object-Relational Mapper), the layer between your JavaScript/TypeScript code and the SQL database, and it provides three things that work together:
- a **type-safe query client:** you query the database in TypeScript (`prisma.user.findMany(...)`) and get *typed* results, so the compiler catches mistakes (a wrong field name, a type error) before they run, a huge reliability win over writing raw SQL strings.
- a **schema definition language:** `schema.prisma` is the *single source of truth* for your database structure (your tables, fields, and relationships), written in a clear declarative format.
- a **migration system:** when you change the schema, Prisma generates the SQL migration to update the database to match.
The schema is the linchpin: from it, Prisma *generates the TypeScript types* (so your code is type-safe against the actual data shape) *and generates the migration SQL* (so the database structure stays in sync with the schema). You define your data once, in the schema, and Prisma keeps both your code's types and your database's structure aligned with it.

## Where this fits
This week builds the data layer of the Backend phase: PostgreSQL (the production database), Prisma (type-safe queries, schema, migrations), and the data-modelling skill (schemas, indexes, migrations) that gives your backend a robust foundation. It is FORGE's own stack. Today's orientation: move from SQLite to PostgreSQL for real concurrency, network access, and tooling; use Prisma as the type-safe ORM with the schema as the single source of truth that generates both types and migrations; and design data carefully because it is costly to change later. Tomorrow you learn Postgres fundamentals.

items.title: Postgres fundamentals
items.body:
## PostgreSQL fundamentals: tables, types, relationships
PostgreSQL is a **relational database**: data lives in **tables** (rows and columns), each column has a **type** (text, integer, boolean, timestamp, etc.), and tables **relate** to each other via keys. The fundamentals to understand:
```sql
-- a table with typed columns and a primary key
CREATE TABLE users (
  id         SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,        -- unique identifier for each row
  email      TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,       -- must be unique, must exist
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now()
);
-- a related table: each order belongs to a user (a foreign key)
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id      SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INTEGER REFERENCES users(id),  -- links to a user
  total   NUMERIC NOT NULL
);
```
(You will define these via Prisma's schema, not raw SQL, but understanding the underlying concepts, tables, types, keys, relationships, is essential, because Prisma is a layer *over* this.) The key ideas: a **primary key** uniquely identifies each row; a **foreign key** links a row to a row in another table (an order *belongs to* a user); and **constraints** (`NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`) enforce rules about valid data.

## Relationships and data integrity: the heart of relational design
The defining power of a relational database, and the heart of good data modelling, is **relationships** and the **data integrity** the database enforces. Real data is connected, users *have* orders, orders *have* items, a blog post *has* comments, and you model these connections with foreign keys that link tables. This relational structure lets you store each piece of data *once* and link to it (a user's details live in one place, referenced by all their orders), which is **normalisation**, avoiding duplicating the same data across rows (where it would get inconsistent). And the database *enforces integrity*: a foreign key constraint means an order *cannot* reference a non-existent user (the database rejects it), a `UNIQUE` constraint means two users cannot share an email, a `NOT NULL` means a required field cannot be empty. This enforcement is hugely valuable: the *database itself* guarantees your data stays valid and consistent, regardless of bugs in the application code, so you cannot accidentally create an order for a deleted user or two accounts with the same email. Designing the right tables, relationships, and constraints, modelling your domain's entities and how they connect, with the database enforcing the rules, is the core data-modelling skill, and getting it right gives you a foundation where invalid data is *impossible*, not just discouraged. This is "data you won't regret": a well-modelled, constraint-enforced schema prevents whole categories of data corruption.

## Think about your data model deliberately
The practical wisdom is to **design the data model thoughtfully up front**, because, as the week's title stresses, data design is costly to change later, the whole application is built on the schema, and migrating a poorly-designed schema with live data is painful. So you invest in getting the model right: What are the *entities* (users, orders, products, posts)? What are their *fields* and *types*? How do they *relate* (one user has many orders; a post has many comments)? What *constraints* enforce validity (unique emails, required fields, valid references)? Thinking this through, ideally sketching the entities and relationships before writing code (the data-modelling equivalent of the architecture-on-paper discipline), produces a schema that is normalised, constraint-protected, and matches how the domain actually works, which supports the app cleanly as it grows. The contrast is a schema thrown together field-by-field as you go, which accumulates duplication, missing constraints, and awkward relationships that you fight forever. Data modelling rewards the deliberate, think-first approach more than almost any other part of web development, because the cost of a mistake is so high and so lasting. Understanding Postgres fundamentals, tables, types, keys, relationships, constraints, and integrity, gives you the vocabulary to design that model well, which is the foundation of a regret-free data layer.

## Where this fits
You understand PostgreSQL fundamentals: typed tables, primary and foreign keys, relationships, and constraints, with the database *enforcing data integrity* (valid references, uniqueness, required fields) so invalid data is impossible, and the discipline of designing the data model deliberately up front because it is costly to change. Tomorrow you make queries fast with indexes.

items.body: EXPLAIN ANALYZE your slowest query before adding an index. What was the cost? After adding the index? When does the index hurt?

items.title: Indexes
items.body:
## Indexes: making queries fast
As data grows, *how fast* the database can find what you ask for matters enormously, and **indexes** are the primary tool for query performance. Without an index, finding rows that match a condition (e.g. `WHERE email = '...'`) requires the database to *scan every row* (a "full table scan"), which is fine for a hundred rows and catastrophic for a million. An **index** is a separate data structure that lets the database *find* matching rows quickly without scanning everything, like the index at the back of a book lets you find a topic without reading every page:
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);   -- now lookups by email are fast
```
With the index, `WHERE email = '...'` jumps near-directly to the matching rows; without it, the database reads the whole table. For any column you frequently *search, filter, join, or sort by*, an index can turn a slow query into an instant one.

## When to index, and the trade-off
Indexes are powerful but not free, and understanding the trade-off is what makes you use them well rather than blindly:
- **Index the columns you query by:** foreign keys (used in joins), columns in `WHERE` filters, columns you sort by, and unique columns (email). These are where an index turns a full scan into a fast lookup, a potentially enormous speedup on large tables.
- **The cost:** each index takes *storage* and, more importantly, *slows down writes* (every insert/update/delete must also update the indexes), so indexes trade faster reads for slower writes and more space. This means you do *not* index every column reflexively, an index on a column you never query by is pure cost with no benefit, and too many indexes can noticeably slow writes.
- **The judgement:** add indexes for the queries your application actually runs (the columns it searches/filters/joins/sorts by), and measure, the database's query analysis (`EXPLAIN`) shows whether a query is using an index or doing a full scan, so you can find the slow queries and add the indexes that fix them.
So indexing is a deliberate, query-driven optimisation: you index the columns your real queries depend on, accepting the write/storage cost where the read speedup is worth it, and you skip indexes that no query uses.

## Indexing as performance thinking, measured
The deeper lesson indexes teach is *performance thinking for data*, and it follows the same measure-then-optimise discipline as performance work across the whole track. The naive approach is either to ignore indexes (and watch the app slow to a crawl as data grows, with no idea why) or to index everything (wasting storage and slowing writes). The right approach is *measured and query-driven*: understand which queries your app runs and on which columns, index those columns so the common queries are fast, and use the database's tools (`EXPLAIN`, slow-query logs) to *find* the queries that are doing full scans and fix the specific ones that matter. This is exactly the "don't optimise prematurely, measure to find the real bottleneck, fix that" rigor from the React-performance and ML-performance lessons, now for the database: most query slowness on a growing app is a missing index on a frequently-queried column, and the fix is targeted (add *that* index), found by measuring (the query plan shows the scan). Indexes are also one of the highest-leverage performance tools you have, a single well-placed index can turn a multi-second query into a millisecond one, which is why understanding them is essential for any app whose data grows. Knowing that indexes speed reads at the cost of writes/storage, that you index the columns your real queries use, and that you find the queries to optimise by measuring, is the performance foundation of a data layer that stays fast as it scales, part of designing data you won't regret (a schema that is fast as well as correct).

## Where this fits
You understand indexes: separate structures that let the database find rows fast without scanning the whole table, indexed on the columns your queries actually search/filter/join/sort by, trading faster reads for slower writes and storage, applied with the measure-then-optimise discipline (find slow full-scan queries via `EXPLAIN`, add the index that fixes them). Tomorrow you work with all of this through Prisma, the type-safe ORM.

items.title: Prisma
items.body:
## Prisma: querying with type safety
Now you work with Postgres through **Prisma**, which lets you define your data and query it in TypeScript with full type safety. You define the schema declaratively, and Prisma generates a typed client:
```prisma
// schema.prisma -- the single source of truth
model User {
  id      Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
  email   String  @unique
  orders  Order[]                 // a relationship: one user has many orders
}
model Order {
  id      Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
  total   Decimal
  user    User    @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
  userId  Int
}
```
```ts
// queries are type-safe TypeScript:
const users = await prisma.user.findMany({ where: { email: 'a@b.com' }, include: { orders: true } });
// `users` is fully typed; a typo in a field name is a compile error
```
The schema declares your models, fields, types, and relationships (the same relational concepts from D2, in Prisma's clean syntax), and from it Prisma generates a *typed* client so every query is checked against your actual data shape.

## Why type safety transforms working with data
Prisma's type safety is its standout benefit, and understanding *why* it matters so much shows what it eliminates. Without an ORM, you write SQL as *strings* (`"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ..."`), which the compiler cannot check, so a misspelled column, a wrong type, a query that does not match the actual table, all fail only at *runtime*, often in production, as a class of avoidable bugs. With Prisma, your queries are *TypeScript*, checked against the schema-generated types at *compile time*: a wrong field name, a type mismatch, a relationship that does not exist, are caught *before the code runs*, in your editor, with autocomplete guiding you to the right fields. This catches a whole category of data-access bugs at development time, dramatically improving reliability, and it makes working with the database far more pleasant (autocomplete for your tables and fields, the compiler as a safety net). The schema-as-single-source-of-truth is key: because the types are *generated from* the schema, your code's understanding of the data and the actual database structure *cannot drift apart*, change the schema and the types update, so any query that no longer matches is immediately flagged. This alignment, code types and database structure always in sync, derived from one schema, is what makes Prisma so effective and is a major reliability upgrade over raw SQL strings.

## ORM convenience, with awareness of what's underneath
Prisma also makes *working* with relational data convenient, handling relationships (`include: { orders: true }` fetches a user with their orders, no manual join SQL), providing a clean API for the common operations (find, create, update, delete, filter, sort), and managing the connection, so you write expressive TypeScript instead of hand-assembling SQL. The discipline, as with every abstraction, is to use Prisma's convenience *while understanding the SQL and database concepts underneath* (which is exactly why you learned Postgres fundamentals and indexes first). This matters because an ORM can hide performance pitfalls if used naively, the classic is the *N+1 query problem* (fetching a list and then a separate query per item for its related data, turning one operation into hundreds of queries), which Prisma can cause if you are not deliberate (and solves with `include`/proper fetching when you are). Knowing what SQL Prisma generates, and that your queries hit a real database with real performance characteristics (where indexes from D3 matter), keeps you from the trap of treating the ORM as magic that makes the database disappear. So you get Prisma's real benefits, type safety, convenience, schema-as-truth, while retaining the underlying understanding (SQL, joins, indexes, query cost) that lets you use it *well* and debug it when a query is slow. This is the same "use the abstraction, understand the layer beneath" judgement from across the track, and for the data layer it is especially important because data performance and correctness are so consequential.

## Where this fits
You can work with Postgres through Prisma: a declarative schema as the single source of truth, generating a type-safe client so data-access bugs are caught at compile time, with convenient relationship handling, used while understanding the SQL and performance (joins, indexes, N+1) underneath. Tomorrow you handle how the schema *evolves* safely: migrations.
