weeks.title: File Uploads, Object Storage, and CDNs
weeks.context:
Storing files is not the same as storing data. Database rows are structured and indexed, they are designed for queries. Files are binary blobs that can be gigabytes. Storing them in your database (as BLOBs) works at small scale and is a mess at large scale. The standard architecture: store files in object storage, store the file metadata (URL, size, type, owner) in your database.

Object storage is the category. S3 is Amazon's implementation and the industry standard for the API. Every major cloud has an S3-compatible service: Cloudflare R2 (no egress fees, good choice for most apps), Backblaze B2, DigitalOcean Spaces, Google Cloud Storage. They all implement the same API. The Cloudflare R2 SDK is the AWS SDK with a different endpoint URL, the client code is identical.

Presigned URLs are the right way to handle uploads in a web application. The naive approach: browser uploads file to your server, your server uploads to S3. Problems: your server handles the bandwidth and compute cost, your server is in the critical path, large files can time out. The correct approach: browser asks your server for a presigned URL (a time-limited signed URL that allows a specific upload action), your server generates the presigned URL using the SDK, the browser uploads directly to S3 using that URL, your server is not in the upload path. Your server only handles metadata.

Image optimisation. Next.js has a built-in Image component that handles optimisation, it serves images in WebP or AVIF format (smaller than JPEG/PNG), resizes images to the displayed size (no serving a 2000px image in a 200px container), and lazy loads images below the fold. For user-uploaded images, you typically process them on the server after upload: resize to a maximum dimension, convert to WebP, generate thumbnail variants. Libraries: sharp (fast, native Node module).

Content Delivery Networks cache your static assets at edge locations close to your users. Without a CDN, every user downloads the original file from your single origin server, regardless of geography. With a CDN, the first request to each edge location fetches from origin and caches; subsequent requests are served from the edge, much faster for global audiences. Cloudflare R2 includes CDN functionality. AWS CloudFront sits in front of S3.

This week: add avatar upload to Bean Forge user profiles and menu item image upload to the admin panel using presigned URLs and Cloudflare R2.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Storing files is not storing data
Apps handle files, profile pictures, document uploads, product images, attachments, and storing files is *not* the same as storing data, a distinction that shapes the whole architecture. Database rows are *structured and indexed*, designed for *queries* (find users where email = ...). Files are *binary blobs* that can be megabytes or gigabytes, and you do not query *into* them. Storing files *in* your database (as BLOBs) works at small scale but becomes a mess at large scale (bloated database, slow backups, poor performance). The standard, correct architecture separates them: **store the files in object storage, and store the file *metadata* (URL, size, type, owner) in your database**. This week you learn that architecture, object storage (S3 and compatible services), presigned uploads, CDNs, image optimisation, and validation, the right way to handle files in a real app.

## The standard architecture: files in object storage, metadata in the database
The core pattern to internalise is the *separation* of the file's *bytes* from the file's *record*:
```text
DATABASE (your Postgres):   the file's METADATA (a row)
   { id, filename, url, size, contentType, ownerId, uploadedAt }
OBJECT STORAGE (S3/R2):     the file's actual BYTES (the blob itself)
   the image/document/video, stored as an object, served via its URL
```
The database holds a *row* describing the file (who owns it, its name, type, size, and the *URL* where the bytes live) that you can query, list, and relate like any data, while the actual file *content* lives in **object storage**, a service built for storing and serving large blobs cheaply and at scale. The database row *points to* the file in object storage (via the URL), so you query and manage files through their metadata rows while the heavy bytes live where they belong. This separation is the foundation: the database does what it is good at (structured, queryable metadata) and object storage does what *it* is good at (storing and serving large files), each used for its strength.

## Why this separation, concretely
Understanding *why* you separate files from the database (rather than storing files as BLOBs in it) shows the architecture's value:
- **Databases are not built for large blobs:** storing big files in the database bloats it, slows queries and backups, and wastes the database's expensive, query-optimised storage on inert bytes you never query into. Object storage is *built* for blobs, cheap, scalable, durable storage of large files, so files belong there.
- **Serving files efficiently:** object storage (often paired with a CDN, D-later) serves files directly and efficiently to users (and can scale to huge traffic), whereas serving large files *through* your application/database is slow and burdens your server. Files served from object storage/CDN do not consume your app server's resources.
- **Scale and cost:** object storage scales to enormous amounts of data cheaply and handles the durability/redundancy of files, which a database doing double-duty as a file store does poorly and expensively.
- **Clean separation of concerns:** metadata (queryable, relational) in the database, bytes (large, served directly) in object storage, each system used for what it does best, which keeps both performant.
So the standard architecture, files in object storage, metadata in the database, is not arbitrary: it puts each kind of data where it is handled best, keeping the database lean and fast and the file storage scalable and cheap, which is essential as file volume grows. Storing files in the database might seem simpler at first, but it is the classic "works small, breaks at scale" trap that this architecture avoids.

## Where this fits
This week handles file storage in the Real-World Features phase: object storage (S3 and compatible), presigned/direct uploads, image optimisation, validation, and CDNs, the correct way to handle the files that real apps deal with. It builds on your data layer (metadata in the database) and serving knowledge. Today's orientation: storing files is not storing data, so the standard architecture stores files in *object storage* (built for large blobs) and their *metadata* in your database (queryable rows pointing to the files), using each system for its strength and avoiding the database-as-file-store trap. Tomorrow you learn object storage itself: S3 and S3-compatible services.

items.title: S3 and S3-compatible services
items.body:
## Object storage: S3 and its compatible ecosystem
**Object storage** is the category of service for storing files (objects) at scale, and **S3** (Amazon's Simple Storage Service) is the implementation that became the industry standard, so much so that its *API* is a de facto standard that other providers implement. The key facts:
```text
S3 (Amazon)  - the original, the industry-standard API
S3-compatible services (same API, different provider):
  Cloudflare R2     - NO egress fees (great for most apps)
  Backblaze B2, DigitalOcean Spaces, Google Cloud Storage, ...
```
The remarkable thing is that these are all *S3-API-compatible*: they implement the *same* API, so your code is essentially *identical* across them, the Cloudflare R2 SDK *is* the AWS SDK with a different endpoint URL, and the client code does not change. You upload, download, list, and delete *objects* (files) in *buckets* (containers), using the standard S3 operations, regardless of which provider you choose.

## Why S3-compatibility matters, and choosing a provider
The S3-API-as-standard situation has real practical value, and understanding it helps you choose well:
- **Portability and no lock-in:** because the API is standard, you can *switch providers* by changing configuration (the endpoint URL and credentials), not rewriting code, so you are not locked into one vendor. You learn *one* API (S3's) and it works everywhere.
- **Choosing on cost and features, not API:** since the API is the same, you pick a provider based on *cost and features* rather than code compatibility, and a major cost factor is **egress fees** (charges for *downloading*/serving data out). Here **Cloudflare R2** stands out: it has *no egress fees*, which is a big deal because serving files (egress) can be the dominant cost for a file-heavy app, so R2 is an excellent, cost-effective choice for most apps (the same kind of cost-driven infrastructure decision as elsewhere). AWS S3 charges egress, which can get expensive at scale; R2 and some others do not.
- **The standard operations:** across all of them you work with *buckets* (containers for objects) and *objects* (your files), using standard operations (put, get, list, delete), so the mental model is consistent.
So you learn the S3 API (universal), and choose a provider based on cost (egress fees especially, where R2's lack of them is compelling) and features, knowing you can switch later if needed. This is a clean example of an API standard enabling portability and cost-based choice, and it means file storage is one less thing to be locked into.

## Access control and security for files
A crucial aspect of object storage to get right is **access control**, who can read and write your files, because misconfigured file storage is a *very* common and serious security mistake. The key concepts:
- **Buckets/objects can be private or public:** most user files should be *private* by default (a user's uploaded document should not be readable by anyone with the URL), accessible only through controlled means (presigned URLs, D4), while some files (public images) may be public. The dangerous, classic mistake is making a bucket *publicly readable* (or writable) when it should not be, exposing private user files to the world (there have been many real breaches from misconfigured public S3 buckets leaking sensitive data).
- **Credentials are secrets:** your storage access keys are secrets (env vars, never committed, like all secrets), and you scope them with least privilege (the app's credentials should allow only what it needs).
- **Controlled access via presigned URLs (D4):** rather than making files public, you grant *temporary, specific* access to a private file via a presigned URL, the secure pattern.
So you treat file storage with the same security care as everything else: private by default, secrets protected, least privilege, and *no* accidentally-public buckets of private data, this access-control discipline is essential because file storage breaches (leaked private files from misconfiguration) are common and damaging. Object storage gives you scalable, cheap, portable file storage; using it *securely* (correct access control) is the responsibility that comes with it.

## Where this fits
You understand object storage: S3 and the S3-compatible ecosystem (same API across providers, so you choose on cost, especially egress fees, where Cloudflare R2's lack of them is compelling, and avoid lock-in), working with buckets and objects, and the critical *access control* discipline (private by default, protected credentials, no accidentally-public private files). Tomorrow you handle a common file type with special needs: image optimisation.

items.title: Image optimisation
items.body:
## Image optimisation: serving images efficiently
Images are the most common uploaded files and the biggest contributors to slow, heavy pages, so **image optimisation** (serving images efficiently) is essential for performance. A raw uploaded image (a multi-megapixel phone photo) is *far* larger than needed for displaying on a web page, and serving it as-is wastes bandwidth and slows load dramatically. Optimisation means transforming images to the *right* size, format, and quality for how they are displayed:
```text
raw upload:        4000x3000, 8MB JPEG (a phone photo)
optimised for web: resized to the display size, modern format (WebP/AVIF),
                   compressed, maybe multiple sizes for different screens
-> often 10-50x smaller, visually identical at display size
```
The key techniques: **resize** to the dimensions actually displayed (don't serve a 4000px image into a 400px slot), **convert to modern formats** (WebP, AVIF, much smaller than JPEG/PNG at the same quality), **compress** appropriately, and serve **responsive sizes** (different sizes for different screens, so a phone gets a small image, a desktop a larger one).

## Why image optimisation matters so much for performance
Image optimisation is one of the highest-impact performance optimisations for most web apps, and understanding why shows its importance:
- **Images dominate page weight:** on most pages, images are by far the largest assets, so unoptimised images are usually the single biggest cause of slow page loads (the "Web Vitals" performance you will formalise in W18 is heavily affected by image loading). Optimising images often improves load time more than any other single change.
- **The savings are enormous:** serving an appropriately-sized, modern-format, compressed image instead of a raw upload can be *10-50x* smaller for the *same visual result* at display size, which is a massive bandwidth and load-time reduction for no quality loss the user notices. This directly improves perceived speed, user experience, and (for the cost-conscious) bandwidth costs.
- **It compounds:** every image on every page for every user, so optimising images has a large cumulative effect on the whole app's performance and cost.
So image optimisation is not a minor tweak, it is often *the* most impactful performance work for an image-containing app, turning slow, heavy pages into fast ones by serving images at the size, format, and quality actually needed rather than the bloated originals. This connects to the perceived-performance and Web-Vitals themes: fast-loading images are central to a fast-feeling site, and unoptimised images are the most common reason sites feel slow.

## How to optimise: tools and the right architecture
Practically, you do *not* hand-optimise every image, you use tools and services that optimise on the fly or at upload, which is the right architecture. The options:
- **Image CDN / transformation services** (Cloudflare Images, imgix, Cloudinary, or your framework's image handling like Next.js's `<Image>`, FORGE's stack): these optimise images *automatically and on demand*, you store the original, and the service serves resized, format-converted, compressed versions per request (the right size for the requesting device, in the best format the browser supports), often cached at a CDN. This is the modern, recommended approach: store originals, let an image service deliver optimised versions automatically.
- **Optimise at upload:** alternatively, generate optimised versions (and thumbnails) when a file is uploaded, storing several sizes.
- **Responsive images:** serve the appropriate size per device (via `srcset` or the image service), so each client downloads only what it needs.
The principle is to *automate* image optimisation (via an image service/CDN or upload-time processing) rather than serving raw uploads, and to serve each user the right-sized, modern-format, compressed image for their context. This delivers the large performance wins automatically, without manual work per image, and it is standard practice for any serious app (and built into frameworks like Next.js that FORGE uses). Getting image optimisation right, automated, responsive, modern-format, is one of the most effective things you can do for an app's performance, which is why it is its own focus in handling files.

## Where this fits
You understand image optimisation: serving images at the right size, modern format (WebP/AVIF), and compression for how they are displayed, which is often the *highest-impact* performance optimisation (images dominate page weight; savings are 10-50x), automated via image CDN/transformation services or upload-time processing rather than serving raw uploads. Tomorrow you handle uploading files efficiently: direct-to-storage uploads with progress.

items.title: Direct-to-S3 uploads with progress tracking
items.body:
## Direct-to-storage uploads with presigned URLs
How do files get *into* object storage? The naive way, the user uploads to your server, which then uploads to storage, is wasteful (the file passes through your server, consuming its bandwidth and memory, a bottleneck for large files and many users). The right way is **direct-to-storage uploads** using **presigned URLs**: your server generates a temporary, signed URL that grants permission to upload *one specific file* directly to storage, and the client uploads *straight to object storage*, bypassing your server:
```text
1. client tells your server "I want to upload a file" (name, type, size)
2. your server generates a PRESIGNED URL (a temporary, signed permission to upload to a specific object)
3. server returns the presigned URL to the client
4. client uploads the file DIRECTLY to object storage using that URL (not through your server)
5. client notifies your server the upload is done; server saves the metadata row
```
The file goes directly from the user to storage, and your server only handles the small coordination (issuing the presigned URL, saving metadata), never the heavy file bytes.

## Why presigned, direct uploads are the right pattern
Understanding why this pattern is correct shows the architecture's value:
- **Your server is not a bottleneck:** the large file bytes never pass through your application server, so uploading a 100MB file does not consume your server's bandwidth, memory, or request time, the upload goes user-to-storage directly, and your server stays free to handle other requests. This is essential for scale (many users uploading large files would otherwise overwhelm your server).
- **Secure, scoped permission:** the presigned URL grants *temporary, specific* permission, upload *this* object, for a *short* time, without making the bucket public or exposing your storage credentials to the client. The client gets exactly the access it needs (upload one file) and no more, which is why files can stay *private* (D2's access control) while still allowing uploads. The same presigned-URL mechanism also grants temporary *read* access to private files (a short-lived download URL).
- **Progress tracking:** because the client uploads directly, it can track *upload progress* (the browser knows how much of the file it has sent) and show a progress bar, which is important UX for large-file uploads (the user sees it working). 
So presigned direct uploads are efficient (server not a bottleneck), secure (scoped temporary permission, files stay private), and good UX (progress tracking), the right way to handle uploads, especially at scale or for large files. Your server's role shrinks to coordinating (issue the URL, record the metadata), which is exactly what it should do.

## Progress, robustness, and the upload UX
Building good uploads also means handling the *experience and robustness* of uploading, which presigned direct uploads enable. **Progress tracking**: since the client uploads directly to storage, it can monitor and display upload progress (a progress bar, "60%"), essential for large files so the user knows it is working and how long is left, a much better experience than a frozen "uploading..." with no feedback (the same "feedback is part of the feature" principle from forms). **Robustness**: uploads can fail (network drops, especially for large files on mobile), so good upload handling considers retries and clear error feedback, and for very large files, *resumable/chunked* uploads (uploading in parts so a failure doesn't restart the whole thing) are the robust approach. **Validation** (tomorrow, D5) also fits here: you validate the file (type, size) before/at upload. The overall pattern, client requests permission, server issues a scoped presigned URL, client uploads directly with progress, server records metadata, handling failures gracefully, is how real apps handle uploads well: efficient, secure, and with good UX. This keeps your server lean (it never touches the bytes), your storage secure (private, scoped access), and your users informed (progress) and unblocked (robust to failures). Getting uploads right with presigned URLs and good progress/error handling is a notable step up from the naive "POST the file to my server" approach, and it is what scales and what users experience as smooth.

## Where this fits
You understand direct-to-storage uploads via presigned URLs: the client uploads files *directly* to object storage using a temporary scoped permission your server issues, so your server is not a bottleneck, files stay private/secure, and the client can show upload progress, with robustness (retries, resumable for large files) for good UX. Tomorrow you handle a security-critical part of uploads: file validation.

items.title: File validation
items.body:
## File validation: never trust uploaded files
Accepting file uploads means accepting *untrusted input* from users (and potentially attackers), so **file validation** is a security-critical discipline: you must validate uploaded files (type, size, content) and never blindly trust them, because malicious or malformed uploads are a real attack vector. The validations:
```text
- SIZE:    enforce a maximum (reject a 5GB upload to a profile-picture field)
- TYPE:    verify the file is actually the allowed type (an image upload should be a real image),
           and crucially check the ACTUAL content, not just the filename/extension or claimed type
- CONTENT: for images, confirm it's a valid image; reject anything unexpected
- never execute or trust uploaded files; store them safely (private, not in a web-executable path)
```
Validation happens both client-side (for quick UX feedback) and, *essentially*, server-side (the real security check, since client-side checks can be bypassed, the same "server-side enforcement is the real security" lesson from auth).

## Why file uploads are a serious attack vector
Understanding *why* unvalidated uploads are dangerous shows why validation is non-negotiable:
- **Malicious file content:** an attacker can upload a file that is *not* what it claims, a script disguised as an image, a malicious payload, a file crafted to exploit a vulnerability in image processing, and if your app trusts the claimed type or executes/serves the file carelessly, this can lead to serious attacks (code execution, serving malware to other users, exploiting a parser). The classic danger is an uploaded file being *executed* or *served as active content*, so you never store uploads in a location where they could be executed, and you verify the *actual* content type, not just the extension (an attacker renaming `evil.php` to `image.jpg` should not fool you, so you check the real content, not the filename).
- **Resource abuse:** without a size limit, an attacker (or a careless user) uploads enormous files to consume your storage and bandwidth (a denial-of-service / cost attack), so size limits are essential.
- **Malformed files causing crashes:** a corrupted or maliciously-malformed file can crash your processing (e.g. an image library choking on a crafted file), so validating that files are well-formed (and handling processing errors) prevents this.
- **Storing/serving harmful content:** an uploaded file might be malware or inappropriate content that you would then serve to *other* users, so validation (and sometimes scanning) protects your users too.
So uploads are a genuine, well-known attack surface, and the validation, real content-type verification (not just extension), size limits, well-formedness checks, safe storage (private, non-executable), server-side enforcement, is what makes accepting user files safe rather than a vulnerability. This is the "public-facing input will be abused, validate it" discipline (from the contact form's spam protection, and pervasive in security) applied to files, where the stakes are high because files can carry executable or malicious content.

## The discipline: treat uploads as hostile until validated
The broader lesson is the security mindset that **all user input is untrusted, and file uploads are an especially dangerous form of it, so you treat uploaded files as potentially hostile until validated**, which is foundational security thinking. The naive view is "the user uploaded a profile picture, store it"; the security view is "an untrusted party sent me an arbitrary file claiming to be an image, which I must validate (real type, size, well-formedness), store safely (private, non-executable), and serve carefully, before trusting it at all." This connects to the recurring security theme across the track (validate input, server-side enforcement, anticipate abuse, the broken-access-control and injection lessons): files are just another untrusted input, with the added danger that they are *content* that might be executed or served, so the validation and safe-handling discipline is critical. Concretely: validate type by actual content (not the claimed extension/MIME), enforce size limits, verify well-formedness, store uploads privately and never in an executable path, serve them safely (correct content-type headers, often from a separate domain to limit damage), and enforce all of this *server-side*. Treating uploads as hostile-until-validated, with this defensive handling, is what lets an app safely accept user files, and skipping it (trusting the claimed type, no size limit, executing or carelessly serving uploads) is how upload-based breaches happen. File validation is the security responsibility that comes with the convenience of letting users upload, and getting it right is essential for any app that accepts files.

## Where this fits
You understand file validation: treating uploaded files as untrusted, potentially hostile input, validating their actual content type (not the extension), size, and well-formedness, storing them safely (private, non-executable) and serving carefully, enforced server-side, because uploads are a serious attack vector (malicious content, resource abuse, crashes). Tomorrow you handle serving files fast at scale: image services and CDNs.

items.title: Image services
items.body:
## Serving files fast: CDNs and image services
Storing files is one thing; *serving* them fast to users worldwide is another, and the tool is the **CDN** (Content Delivery Network). A CDN is a globally-distributed network of servers that *cache* your files close to users, so a user in Tokyo gets your image from a nearby Tokyo server rather than fetching it across the world from your origin storage:
```text
without a CDN:  every user fetches the file from your one storage location (far away = slow)
with a CDN:     the file is cached at edge servers worldwide;
                each user gets it from a NEARBY edge (fast), origin hit only on cache miss
```
For files, especially images (the bulk of most apps' served bytes), a CDN dramatically improves load speed (files served from a nearby edge) and reduces load/cost on your origin storage (most requests hit the cache, not your storage). Object storage providers integrate with CDNs (Cloudflare R2 with Cloudflare's CDN, etc.), and **image services** (D3's Cloudflare Images, imgix, Cloudinary, Next.js image handling) combine *optimisation* and *CDN delivery*, serving optimised images from a global edge cache.

## Why CDNs matter, and how they combine with optimisation
Understanding the CDN's value, and how it pairs with image optimisation, completes the file-serving picture:
- **Speed via proximity:** the main win is *latency*, serving a file from an edge server geographically near the user is far faster than fetching from a distant origin, which (for image-heavy pages) substantially improves load time and the perceived speed/Web-Vitals you care about. A CDN turns "fast for users near my server, slow for everyone else" into "fast for everyone, everywhere."
- **Offloading the origin:** because the CDN caches and serves most requests, your origin storage handles far fewer requests, which reduces its load and cost (and, with no-egress-fee storage like R2 plus a CDN, can be very cost-effective). The CDN absorbs traffic spikes too (a popular file served from cache scales effortlessly).
- **Combined with optimisation (D3):** the ideal setup *combines* image optimisation and CDN delivery, an image service stores the original, generates the right optimised version (size, format, quality) per request, *and* serves it from a global CDN cache, so users get the *optimally-sized, modern-format, compressed* image from a *nearby* edge. This combination, optimised *and* edge-cached, is what makes images load fast worldwide, and it is why image services (optimisation + CDN in one) are the modern standard.
So a CDN is how you serve files (especially images) fast and cost-effectively at global scale, by caching them close to users, and pairing it with optimisation gives you images that are both *small* (optimised) and *fast to fetch* (edge-cached), the complete recipe for fast file/image serving.

## The full file-handling architecture, and the principle
Stepping back, you can now see the *complete* architecture for handling files well, which ties the week together:
```text
UPLOAD:   client -> (presigned URL) -> directly to OBJECT STORAGE (private, validated)
STORE:    file bytes in object storage; metadata row in the database
OPTIMISE: image service generates right-sized, modern-format versions on demand
SERVE:    via CDN (cached at edges worldwide) -> fast delivery to every user
```
Each piece uses the right tool for its job, object storage for cheap scalable blob storage, the database for queryable metadata, presigned direct uploads so your server isn't a bottleneck, validation for security, optimisation for performance, and a CDN for fast global delivery, and together they form the standard, scalable, secure, fast way to handle files in a real application. The unifying principle is *use the specialised tool for each part of the file lifecycle* (store, secure, optimise, deliver) rather than doing it all naively through your app and database, which gives you file handling that is scalable (object storage + CDN), secure (private + validated + scoped access), fast (optimised + edge-cached), and lean on your server (direct uploads, CDN serving). This is exactly how serious apps handle files, and it is built into modern stacks (Next.js + an image service + R2/S3, close to FORGE's approach). Understanding the full architecture, and *why* each piece is there, is what lets you handle files properly rather than falling into the database-BLOB-and-serve-through-the-app traps that break at scale.

## Where this fits
You understand CDNs and image services: caching files (especially images) at edge servers worldwide for fast, low-latency delivery and origin offloading, combined with optimisation so images are both small and edge-cached, completing the full file-handling architecture (object storage + metadata + presigned uploads + validation + optimisation + CDN), each part using the right specialised tool. Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship a complete file-handling feature.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: proper file handling
You assemble the week into a complete, correct file-handling feature for a real app (image/document uploads), demonstrating the full architecture:
- files in **object storage** (S3-compatible, e.g. R2), **metadata in the database**, with **private access** and presigned URLs.
- **direct-to-storage uploads** via presigned URLs (server not a bottleneck) with **progress** and **server-side validation** (type, size, safety).
- **image optimisation** (right size, modern format) and **CDN** delivery for fast, global serving.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "File handling: object storage + metadata, presigned uploads, validation, optimisation, CDN"
git push
```

## The deliverable is a file system that scales securely and fast
What makes this project demonstrate real competence is that it handles files the *correct, scalable, secure, fast* way, not the naive way that breaks. The strongest version shows the full architecture working: files stored in object storage with metadata in the database (not BLOBs in the database), uploaded *directly* to storage via presigned URLs (so the server isn't a bottleneck), *validated* server-side (so malicious uploads are rejected), kept *private* with scoped access (so files aren't exposed), *optimised* (so images are small) and served via *CDN* (so they load fast worldwide), with upload *progress* for good UX. The proof is that it does the right thing on the dimensions that matter: it would *scale* (object storage + CDN handle volume and traffic), it is *secure* (private, validated, scoped, no public-bucket leak, no malicious-upload execution), and it is *fast* (optimised, edge-cached images). Demonstrating that you understand *why* files go in object storage (not the database), *why* uploads go directly (not through your server), *why* validation is critical, and *how* optimisation and CDNs make serving fast, rather than naively POST-ing files to your server and storing them in the database, is the deliverable, and it is the competence that makes file features in a real app robust rather than a scaling and security liability.

## What file handling established
Step back: you have learned the correct architecture for one of the most common real-app needs, handling user files, with the right tool for each part of the lifecycle. You understand that storing files is not storing data (object storage for bytes, database for metadata), object storage and its portable S3-compatible ecosystem (choosing on cost, especially egress, where R2 shines), image optimisation (the high-impact performance win), presigned direct uploads (efficient, secure, progress-friendly), file validation (the security-critical defence against malicious uploads), and CDNs/image services (fast global delivery). The throughline is *use the specialised tool for each concern* (store, secure, optimise, deliver) to get file handling that scales, stays secure, and serves fast, avoiding the naive traps (database BLOBs, server-as-upload-bottleneck, unvalidated uploads, unoptimised serving) that break real apps. This is standard in serious stacks (and FORGE's image/upload handling), so it is directly real-world relevant.

## Where this fits
You shipped proper file handling, scalable object storage, secure validated direct uploads, optimised CDN serving, the correct architecture for user files. Next week you handle the last Real-World Features capability: **WebSockets and real-time**, for when HTTP's request-response model isn't enough, live chat, real-time updates, collaborative editing, where the *server* needs to push data to connected clients instantly, requiring a persistent, bidirectional connection that HTTP alone cannot provide.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Explain the presigned URL upload flow step by step, including what each party knows and does. Step 1: the browser asks your server for a presigned URL, sending the filename and content type. Step 2: your server validates the request (is the user authenticated? is the file type allowed?), generates a unique S3 key (e.g., users/userId/avatars/randomUUID.webp), calls S3 PutObjectCommand with the key and a 5-minute expiry to generate a presigned URL, and returns the URL and the final public URL of the file to the browser. Step 3: the browser makes a PUT request directly to S3 using the presigned URL, including the file bytes. The presigned URL encodes the allowed bucket, key, content type, and expiry, S3 verifies all of this. Step 4: after the upload succeeds, the browser tells your server the upload is complete, and your server updates the user's avatarUrl in the database to the public URL.

weeks.title: WebSockets and Real-time, When HTTP Isn't Enough
weeks.context:
HTTP is a request-response protocol: the client sends a request, the server sends a response, the connection is done. This model is fine for loading pages and submitting forms. It breaks down when you need the server to push data to connected clients, a live chat message, a real-time dashboard update, a collaborative editing change. For these use cases, you need WebSockets.

A WebSocket is a persistent, bidirectional connection between client and server. It starts as an HTTP connection (the handshake happens over HTTP), then upgrades to the WebSocket protocol. Once upgraded, both sides can send messages to each other at any time without the overhead of a new HTTP connection for each message. The connection stays open until either side closes it.

Socket.IO is the standard Node.js library for WebSockets. It wraps the WebSocket protocol with useful features: automatic reconnection when the connection drops, fallback to long-polling in environments that do not support WebSockets, rooms (named channels where you can broadcast to a subset of connected clients), and namespaces. The server emits events and clients listen for them; clients emit events and the server listens. The programming model is event-driven.

Scaling WebSockets is harder than scaling HTTP. HTTP servers are stateless, any server can handle any request. WebSocket connections are stateful, a connected client is connected to a specific server instance. If you have two server instances and clients connect to both, an event emitted on server 1 is not automatically sent to clients connected to server 2. The solution is an adapter: Socket.IO has a Redis adapter that routes messages between server instances via Redis pub/sub. In development with one server, this does not matter. In production, plan for it.

Server-Sent Events (SSE) are a simpler alternative for one-way server-to-client updates. SSE is a standard HTTP connection that the server keeps open and writes event data to periodically. The client uses the EventSource API. SSE is simpler than WebSockets (no library required, works over HTTP/2), but only supports server-to-client communication. For dashboards, notifications, and activity feeds, SSE is often the better choice.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## When request-response isn't enough
Everything so far used HTTP's **request-response** model: the client sends a request, the server sends a response, done. This is perfect for loading pages and submitting forms, but it has a fundamental limitation, *the server cannot initiate*; it can only *respond* to a client's request. This breaks down when you need the *server to push data to clients* without the client asking: a live chat message arriving, a real-time dashboard updating, a collaborative document changing as others edit, a notification appearing instantly. For these, you need **WebSockets**, a persistent, bidirectional connection where *either side* can send data at *any* time. This week you learn real-time: WebSockets, how to host and scale them, hosted real-time services, and even collaborative-editing data structures, the capabilities that enable live, interactive, multi-user features.

## The WebSocket: a persistent, bidirectional connection
A **WebSocket** is fundamentally different from an HTTP request: it is a *persistent, two-way* connection between client and server that *stays open*, so both sides can send messages whenever they want:
```text
HTTP:       client --request--> server --response--> (connection done)   [client initiates only]
WebSocket:  client <==== persistent open connection ====> server
            either side can send a message at ANY time, no new request needed
            connection stays open until one side closes it
```
A WebSocket *starts* as an HTTP connection (the initial handshake happens over HTTP), then *upgrades* to the WebSocket protocol, and once upgraded, messages flow *both ways* freely without the overhead of a new HTTP request per message. The crucial properties: it is **persistent** (stays open, unlike HTTP's one-shot), **bidirectional** (server can push to client, not just respond), and **low-overhead** (no per-message HTTP request). This is exactly what real-time features need: the server can *push* the new chat message, the dashboard update, the collaborator's edit to the client the instant it happens.

## Why this changes what's possible
Understanding *why* WebSockets enable real-time features clarifies when you need them:
- **Server-initiated updates:** the defining capability, the server can send data to connected clients *without* them asking, so a chat message someone else sent, a price that just changed, a notification, all reach the client *instantly* (pushed), rather than the client having to repeatedly *poll* ("any updates? any updates?") which is wasteful and laggy. Real-time *push* is impossible with pure request-response; WebSockets make it possible.
- **Bidirectional, low-latency interaction:** because the connection is open both ways with low overhead, you get fast, interactive, live communication (you send a chat message, it reaches others instantly; you move your cursor in a collaborative doc, others see it immediately), the responsiveness that live multi-user features require.
- **The right tool for live, multi-user, push-based features:** chat, live dashboards, collaborative editing, multiplayer, live notifications, anything where data changes *for the user* due to *others' or the server's* actions and must appear *immediately*, needs the server-push that WebSockets provide.
So WebSockets unlock a whole category of features (live, real-time, collaborative, push-based) that HTTP's request-response model fundamentally cannot, by providing the persistent, bidirectional, server-can-push connection those features need. Recognising *when* you need real-time (server must push, low-latency multi-user interaction) versus when request-response suffices (most things) is the key judgement.

## Where this fits
This week completes the Real-World Features phase with real-time: WebSockets (the persistent bidirectional connection), hosting and scaling them, hosted real-time services, CRDTs for collaboration, for when HTTP's request-response isn't enough. It is the capability behind live, interactive, multi-user features. Today's orientation: HTTP's request-response can't let the server *push* to clients, which live features (chat, real-time updates, collaboration) need, so WebSockets provide a persistent, bidirectional, low-overhead connection where either side can send at any time. Tomorrow you learn WebSocket basics in practice.

items.title: WebSocket basics
items.body:
## WebSockets in practice: Socket.IO
You build real-time features in Node with **Socket.IO**, the standard Node library for WebSockets, which wraps the raw WebSocket protocol with a friendlier API and important production features. The basic model is *events*: the client and server *emit* named events with data, and *listen* for them, on both sides:
```js
// SERVER
io.on('connection', (socket) => {                 // a client connected
  socket.on('chat message', (msg) => {            // listen for an event from this client
    io.emit('chat message', msg);                  // broadcast it to ALL connected clients
  });
});
// CLIENT
socket.emit('chat message', 'Hello');             // send an event to the server
socket.on('chat message', (msg) => addToChat(msg)); // receive events pushed from the server
```
This event model, `emit` to send, `on` to listen, on both client and server, is the same event-driven pattern you have used throughout (browser events, Node's model), now spanning the persistent connection between client and server. The server can `emit` to one client, or *broadcast* to all (or to a *room*, a subset), which is how a chat message from one user reaches everyone.

## Key real-time concepts Socket.IO gives you
Socket.IO (and real-time work generally) introduces concepts beyond simple send/receive that are essential for real features:
- **Broadcasting and rooms:** you rarely send only to one client; you *broadcast* to all connected clients, or to a *room* (a named group, like a specific chat channel or document), so a message goes to exactly the right set of clients (everyone in this chat room, not every user of the app). Rooms are how you scope real-time updates to the relevant audience.
- **Connection lifecycle:** clients *connect* and *disconnect* (close the tab, lose network), and you handle these events (a user joined, a user left, update the "online" list, clean up). Managing the connection lifecycle (and reconnection when a client drops and comes back) is core to real-time.
- **Reliability features:** Socket.IO adds production-important features over raw WebSockets, *automatic reconnection* (if the connection drops, the client transparently reconnects), and *fallbacks* (if WebSockets aren't available in some environment, it can fall back to other transports), so your real-time feature is robust to the messy reality of networks. This is a key reason to use Socket.IO rather than raw WebSockets.
So building real-time means working with events (emit/on), scoping with rooms/broadcasts, handling the connection lifecycle, and relying on reliability features (reconnection, fallbacks), all of which Socket.IO provides on top of the raw WebSocket protocol, making real-time features practical and robust.

## State and the shift in thinking real-time requires
The deeper shift real-time introduces is in *how you think about state and communication*, which is genuinely different from request-response and worth grasping. In request-response, each interaction is discrete and stateless-ish (a request comes, you respond, done); in real-time, you have *persistent connections* and *shared, live state* across many connected clients that must stay *synchronised* as it changes, which is a more complex, *stateful* model. You are no longer just answering one client's question; you are maintaining a set of live connections and *pushing updates* to keep all the clients' views of shared state consistent in real time (everyone in the chat sees the new message; everyone watching the dashboard sees the update). This means thinking about: *who* should receive each update (rooms/broadcasts), *connection state* (who's connected, handling drops/reconnects), and *keeping clients in sync* as shared state changes. It is a meaningfully different mental model from the request-response world, more like maintaining an ongoing, multi-party live conversation than answering discrete questions, and it brings its own challenges (which the rest of the week addresses: hosting persistent connections, scaling them, handling conflicting concurrent changes in collaboration). Socket.IO gives you the *tools* (events, rooms, lifecycle, reliability); the *shift in thinking* toward persistent connections and live synchronised shared state is what makes real-time a distinct skill. Getting comfortable with this stateful, push-based, multi-client model is the foundation for building real-time features well.

## Where this fits
You can build real-time features with Socket.IO: the event model (emit/on) over persistent connections, broadcasting and rooms to scope updates, connection-lifecycle handling, and reliability features (reconnection, fallbacks), plus the shift in thinking toward persistent connections and live, synchronised shared state across many clients. Tomorrow you handle a real challenge this raises: hosting persistent real-time connections.

items.title: Hosting real-time
items.body:
## Hosting real-time: persistent connections are different
Real-time has a hosting challenge that ordinary web apps don't: **WebSocket connections are persistent and stateful**, which conflicts with how much modern web hosting works. Standard request-response apps suit *stateless, short-lived* request handling (and serverless/edge platforms are built for exactly that, a function spins up, handles a request, spins down). But a WebSocket connection *stays open* for as long as the user is connected (minutes, hours), holding *state* (which clients are connected, which rooms they're in), and this *persistent, stateful* nature is fundamentally at odds with stateless, ephemeral serverless functions:
```text
request-response:  short-lived, stateless -> serverless/edge handles it perfectly
WebSockets:        long-lived, stateful connections -> serverless functions DON'T fit
                   (a function that spins down can't hold an open connection)
```
So hosting real-time requires infrastructure that can *hold persistent connections*, a long-running server (not ephemeral functions), which is a different hosting model from the serverless deployments common for modern web apps (including Next.js/Vercel, FORGE's stack).

## Why this is a real architectural constraint
Understanding *why* persistent connections complicate hosting shows it is a genuine architectural consideration, not a minor config issue:
- **Serverless doesn't hold connections:** serverless functions are designed to be short-lived and stateless (spin up per request, spin down), which is why they scale so well and cost so little for request-response, but a function that spins down *cannot* maintain an open WebSocket connection, so the standard serverless model simply does not support WebSockets directly. This is a real limitation: an app deployed serverless (like a typical Next.js/Vercel app) cannot host WebSocket connections in the serverless functions themselves.
- **You need a persistent server (or a service):** to hold WebSocket connections, you need a *long-running process* (a traditional always-on server, e.g. on Railway, Fly, a VM, or a container that stays up), which is a different deployment model from serverless, *or* you use a hosted real-time *service* (D4) that holds the connections for you. So adding real-time to a serverless app often means running a *separate* persistent service for the WebSocket part, alongside the serverless app.
- **State management across the connection:** the server holding connections also holds connection state (who's connected, rooms), which must be managed, and which complicates scaling (D6, multiple servers each hold *some* connections, so they must coordinate).
So real-time hosting is a real architectural decision: WebSockets need persistent, stateful, long-running infrastructure, which doesn't fit the serverless model that much of modern web hosting (and FORGE) uses, so you either run a dedicated persistent server for the real-time part or use a hosted real-time service. Recognising this constraint, real-time can't just run in your serverless functions, is essential to architecting real-time features correctly, and it is a common surprise ("why can't I just add WebSockets to my Vercel app?").

## The pragmatic implication: separate the real-time concern
The practical takeaway is that **real-time is often best handled as a separate, dedicated concern**, given its different hosting needs, which is a sensible architectural pattern. Rather than forcing your whole app onto persistent-server hosting just to support a real-time feature (losing the benefits of serverless for the rest), you commonly *separate* the real-time part: run the real-time functionality on infrastructure suited to persistent connections (a dedicated long-running server, or a hosted real-time service, D4), while the rest of your app stays on its normal (possibly serverless) hosting, and the two integrate. This is the same "use the right infrastructure for each concern, and separate concerns with different needs" judgement seen throughout (and it echoes how FORGE-style serverless apps add real-time via a dedicated service). It also points strongly toward the *hosted real-time services* (D4) that handle the persistent-connection hosting *for* you, which, for many apps, is the simplest way to add real-time without taking on the burden of running and scaling persistent-connection servers yourself. The key insight to carry: real-time's persistent, stateful nature gives it different hosting requirements than the rest of your (likely serverless) app, so you architect for that, typically by handling real-time as a separate, appropriately-hosted concern rather than trying to cram it into serverless functions that fundamentally can't hold connections. Understanding this constraint up front saves you from the dead-end of trying to run WebSockets where they cannot run, and points you to the right architecture (dedicated server or hosted service) for adding real-time.

## Where this fits
You understand the real-time hosting challenge: WebSocket connections are persistent and stateful, which doesn't fit the stateless, ephemeral serverless model much of modern hosting (and FORGE) uses, so real-time needs long-running infrastructure (a dedicated server) or a hosted service, often handled as a *separate* concern from the rest of your app. Tomorrow you look at the hosted services that solve this for you.

items.title: Hosted real-time services
items.body:
## Hosted real-time services: real-time without the burden
Given that hosting persistent WebSocket connections (and scaling them, D6) is genuinely hard, **hosted real-time services** exist to handle it for you, Pusher, Ably, PartyKit, Supabase Realtime, Liveblocks (for collaboration), and others. These services *hold the WebSocket connections* and provide the real-time infrastructure as a managed product, so you add real-time features *without* running and scaling persistent-connection servers yourself:
```text
hosted real-time service handles:  holding the persistent connections, scaling them,
                                   broadcasting/channels, reliability, global distribution
you handle:                        connecting your clients to it, defining your events/channels,
                                   integrating it with your app's logic
```
Your app (even a serverless one) connects clients to the service and publishes/subscribes to events through it, and the service does the hard part, maintaining all those persistent connections at scale, reliably, globally.

## Why a hosted service is often the right call
The reasoning for using a hosted real-time service is the now-familiar build-vs-buy judgement, and real-time is a strong case for "buy":
- **Persistent-connection infrastructure is hard:** holding many concurrent persistent connections, scaling them across servers (which requires coordination, D6), handling reconnections, global distribution, and reliability, is genuinely difficult infrastructure to build and operate well, and it is *not your app's core value*. A hosted service has specialised in exactly this.
- **It fits serverless apps:** since the service holds the connections, your app doesn't need persistent-connection hosting, so a serverless app (like a Next.js/Vercel app) can have real-time features by connecting to the service, sidestepping the D3 hosting conflict entirely. This is often the *simplest* way to add real-time to a modern (serverless) stack.
- **Scaling is handled:** the service scales the real-time layer for you (D6's hard problem), so you don't build the cross-server coordination that scaling WebSockets yourself requires.
- **Faster and more reliable:** you get robust, scalable, globally-distributed real-time quickly, rather than spending significant effort building and operating connection infrastructure.
So for many apps, especially serverless ones, a hosted real-time service is the pragmatic, right choice: you get the real-time capability without the substantial burden of hosting and scaling persistent connections, focusing on *your* features (the events, channels, and logic) rather than the connection infrastructure. (Specialised services go further, Liveblocks and similar provide ready-made *collaboration* infrastructure including conflict handling, D5.) This is the same "use the specialist for hard, non-differentiating infrastructure" judgement as auth, payments, and email.

## When to self-host vs use a service
The judgement, as always, is to match the approach to your needs. **Use a hosted real-time service** when you want real-time features without operating connection infrastructure (the common case), when your app is serverless (so it can't host connections anyway), when you need it to scale and be reliable without building that yourself, or when you want specialised capability (managed collaboration). **Self-host** (run your own persistent Socket.IO server) when you have specific needs the services don't meet, want full control, have the operational capacity, or are at a scale/cost point where running your own makes sense, but recognise you then own the hard scaling and reliability work (D6). For *most* applications adding real-time features, a hosted service is the sensible default (the burden of self-hosting persistent, scalable connections rarely pays off versus a service), and you reach for self-hosting deliberately when you have a real reason. The deeper point is that real-time, more than most features, has a *high infrastructure burden* (persistent connections at scale), which tilts the build-vs-buy decision strongly toward *buy* (a hosted service) for most apps, you understand WebSockets (so you can use any approach and debug it) but you usually *deploy* real-time via a service that handles the connection infrastructure. Knowing both the underlying technology (WebSockets/Socket.IO) and the practical reality (hosted services usually win for real apps) lets you choose correctly, typically a hosted service, while understanding what it's doing for you.

## Where this fits
You understand hosted real-time services (Pusher, Ably, PartyKit, Liveblocks, and others) that hold and scale the persistent connections for you, the pragmatic, usually-right way to add real-time, especially to serverless apps, sidestepping the hosting/scaling burden, while self-hosting is for specific needs. Tomorrow you handle the hardest part of one real-time use case, collaboration: conflict-free data with CRDTs.

items.title: Conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs)
items.body:
## Collaborative editing and the conflict problem: CRDTs
The hardest real-time use case is **collaborative editing**, multiple people editing the *same* thing (a document, a design) *simultaneously*, because it raises a genuinely hard problem: *conflicts*. When two users edit the same content at the same time, their changes can conflict (both edit the same sentence, both insert at the same spot), and you must *merge* these concurrent changes into a single consistent result that everyone sees, without losing edits or producing garbage. **CRDTs** (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) are data structures *designed* to solve exactly this:
```text
problem:  user A and user B edit the same doc at the same time -> their changes conflict
          how do you merge them so everyone ends up with the SAME, sensible result?
CRDT:     a data structure where concurrent changes ALWAYS merge automatically
          into a consistent result, no central coordinator needed, no lost edits
```
A CRDT is built so that no matter the order or timing in which concurrent edits arrive at different users, they *converge* to the same final state automatically, which is what makes real-time collaboration work.

## Why concurrent collaboration is genuinely hard
Understanding *why* collaboration needs special data structures shows the depth of the problem:
- **Concurrent changes conflict, and naive approaches fail:** if two people edit at once and you just apply changes in arrival order, you get lost edits (one overwrites the other), inconsistency (different users see different results), or corruption (changes that assumed different starting states clash). The "last write wins" naive approach *loses* people's work, which is unacceptable for collaboration.
- **No single source of truth at the moment of edit:** in real-time collaboration, each user is editing their *local* copy and changes propagate, so there isn't one authority applying changes in a clean order, edits happen concurrently on different copies and must be *reconciled*. This is fundamentally a *distributed systems* problem (concurrent changes to replicated state), which is genuinely hard.
- **You need automatic, consistent merging:** the requirement is that *all* users' concurrent edits merge into a *single consistent result* that *everyone converges to*, automatically (you can't ask users to resolve every conflict), without losing anyone's contribution. Achieving this reliably is the hard part.
CRDTs solve this by being mathematically designed so that concurrent operations *commute* (can be applied in any order with the same result) and always *converge*, so edits merge automatically and consistently no matter the timing, which is exactly the guarantee collaboration needs. (An older approach, Operational Transformation, solves the same problem differently and powers some collaborative editors; CRDTs are the increasingly-popular modern approach, e.g. via libraries like Yjs.)

## Use the right tool, and know when you need it
The crucial practical lessons about CRDTs (and collaboration) are about *using* them appropriately, not implementing them, and *recognising when you need them*:
- **Don't build CRDTs yourself, use proven libraries:** CRDTs are subtle, advanced data structures (real distributed-systems theory), so you use battle-tested implementations (Yjs is the standard CRDT library; collaboration services like Liveblocks build on these) rather than rolling your own, the same "don't reinvent hard, subtle infrastructure" judgement as crypto/auth. You understand *what* CRDTs do (automatic conflict-free merging of concurrent edits) so you can use them correctly, but you rely on the libraries for the hard implementation.
- **Know when collaboration (and CRDTs) is actually needed:** true concurrent collaborative editing (Google-Docs-style simultaneous editing) is a *specific, advanced* need, and many "real-time" features *don't* require it, broadcasting messages (chat), pushing updates (a dashboard), or showing presence don't need conflict resolution, because they aren't *concurrent edits to shared state*. So you reach for CRDTs/collaboration infrastructure *only* when you genuinely have the concurrent-editing-of-shared-content problem, not for simpler real-time features (which the earlier days' tools handle). Over-reaching for collaboration machinery when you just need broadcasting is unnecessary complexity.
So the takeaways: collaborative editing is a genuinely hard distributed-systems problem (concurrent conflicting changes), CRDTs are the data structures that solve it (automatic conflict-free convergence), you *use proven libraries/services* rather than building them, and you apply this advanced machinery *only* when you truly need concurrent collaborative editing (not for simpler real-time needs). Understanding the problem and the solution (even at a conceptual level) lets you build collaboration when required, using the right tools, while recognising when your real-time need is simpler. This is the most advanced real-time topic, and knowing it exists and roughly how it works (and when to reach for it) is the valuable part.

## Where this fits
You understand the collaborative-editing conflict problem (concurrent changes to shared content must merge consistently without lost edits) and CRDTs as the data structures that solve it (automatic conflict-free convergence), used via proven libraries (Yjs, collaboration services) rather than built, and *only* when true concurrent collaboration is genuinely needed (not for simpler real-time features). Tomorrow you handle scaling real-time across servers.

items.title: Scaling real-time
items.body:
## Scaling real-time: the multi-server problem
Real-time has a hard scaling problem that ordinary apps don't, and it follows directly from persistent, stateful connections. A single server can hold only so many connections, so at scale you run *multiple* real-time servers, but now the connections are *split across servers*: user A is connected to server 1, user B to server 2, and when A sends a message that B should receive, *server 1 must get it to a client on server 2*, the servers must *coordinate*:
```text
single server:  all clients connected to it -> broadcasting is easy (it has everyone)
multiple servers (needed at scale):  clients split across servers
   user A on server 1 sends a message -> user B on server 2 must receive it
   -> servers must COORDINATE to deliver across the fleet  (the hard part)
```
The standard solution is a shared **pub/sub** backplane (commonly **Redis**): servers publish messages to Redis, and all servers subscribe, so a message from a client on *any* server reaches clients on *all* servers. This coordination layer is what lets multiple real-time servers act as one.

## Why scaling real-time is fundamentally harder than scaling request-response
Understanding *why* real-time scaling is hard (where request-response scaling is comparatively easy) is the key insight:
- **Stateful connections vs stateless requests:** request-response scales easily because it's *stateless*, any server can handle any request (you just add servers behind a load balancer, the stateless property from W9/serverless). Real-time is *stateful*, each server holds specific open connections, so the state (who's connected where) is *distributed across servers*, and you can't just treat any server as interchangeable, the message for user B must reach the *specific* server holding B's connection. This statefulness is what makes scaling hard.
- **Cross-server communication is required:** because connections are split across servers, delivering a message often means routing it *between* servers (to wherever the recipient is connected), which requires the coordination layer (pub/sub via Redis) that stateless request-response never needs. This adds infrastructure and complexity.
- **Connection limits and sticky routing:** each server has a limit on concurrent connections, and clients must *stay* connected to their server (sticky sessions) or reconnect cleanly, adding constraints. Scaling means managing many servers each holding a share of connections, coordinated.
So real-time scaling is fundamentally harder than request-response scaling *because of the persistent, stateful, distributed-across-servers nature of the connections*: you can't just add interchangeable stateless servers, you must coordinate stateful connection-holding servers so messages reach the right clients wherever they're connected, typically via a pub/sub backplane. This is a real distributed-systems problem (the same coordination-across-servers theme as distributed training, multi-agent systems, etc.), and it's exactly why scaling real-time yourself is a significant undertaking.

## Why this makes hosted services even more compelling
The deeper takeaway, tying the week together, is that **the difficulty of scaling real-time is a strong argument for hosted real-time services** (D4), and understanding the scaling problem makes that build-vs-buy case concrete. Scaling real-time yourself means building and operating the multi-server coordination, the pub/sub backplane, sticky routing, connection management across a fleet, handling the stateful distribution, which is substantial, ongoing, specialised infrastructure work. A hosted real-time service *handles all of this for you*: it scales the connections across its own infrastructure, coordinates message delivery globally, and presents you a simple interface, so *you never deal with the multi-server coordination problem at all*. This is precisely why, for most apps, the recommendation is a hosted service: not only does it solve the hosting problem (D3, holding connections), it solves the *scaling* problem (D6, coordinating across servers), both of which are genuinely hard and non-differentiating. So the week's arc lands on a clear judgement: real-time is *conceptually* approachable (WebSockets, events, Socket.IO) but *operationally* hard to host and scale (persistent stateful connections, cross-server coordination), which strongly tilts most real-world real-time toward hosted services that absorb that operational difficulty, you understand the technology and the challenges (so you can build, choose, and debug), but you usually *deploy* real-time via a service precisely because hosting and scaling it yourself is so demanding. Knowing *why* scaling real-time is hard (stateful distributed connections needing coordination) is what makes you appreciate what the services do and choose them wisely, rather than naively trying to scale WebSockets yourself and hitting the coordination wall.

## Where this fits
You understand why scaling real-time is fundamentally hard, persistent, stateful connections split across servers require cross-server coordination (a pub/sub backplane like Redis), unlike easily-scaled stateless request-response, which strongly reinforces the case for hosted real-time services that handle both hosting and scaling for you. Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship a real-time feature.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a real-time feature
You assemble the week into a working real-time feature (live chat, live updates, presence, or a collaborative element), demonstrating real-time done right:
- a **WebSocket**-based feature (via Socket.IO or, more likely, a **hosted real-time service**) where the server *pushes* updates to clients live.
- correct use of **events, broadcasting/rooms**, and **connection-lifecycle** handling, with the real-time concern appropriately hosted (a dedicated service/server, not crammed into serverless).
- if collaborative, proven **CRDT**/collaboration tooling; and an understanding of how it would **scale**.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Real-time feature: WebSocket/hosted-service push, rooms, lifecycle, appropriately hosted"
git push
```

## The deliverable is live, multi-user interaction done right
What makes this project demonstrate real competence is a feature that is *genuinely live and multi-user*, built with the right architecture for real-time's hosting and scaling realities. The strongest version shows the defining real-time capability working, the server *pushes* updates so that something one user does (sends a message, makes a change) appears *instantly* for other users without them refreshing, the live, push-based interaction HTTP can't provide, scoped correctly (the right clients get the update via rooms/broadcast), with connection lifecycle handled (users joining/leaving, reconnection). And crucially, it is *hosted appropriately*: recognising that persistent connections don't fit serverless, you've used a hosted real-time service (or dedicated server) for the real-time part, demonstrating you understand the architectural reality, not just the WebSocket API. The proof is the live experience: open the feature in two browsers and see one's action appear instantly in the other, real-time working, built on infrastructure that suits persistent connections. Demonstrating that you understand *when* real-time is needed (server must push, live multi-user), *how* it works (WebSockets, events, rooms), and *the hosting/scaling realities* (persistent stateful connections, hence dedicated services), rather than naively trying to bolt WebSockets onto serverless, is the deliverable, and it is the competence that lets you add live, interactive features to real apps correctly.

## What real-time, and the Real-World Features phase, established
Step back: you have learned real-time, the capability behind live, interactive, multi-user features, *and* its real operational challenges. You understand when request-response isn't enough (server must push) and WebSockets are needed (persistent, bidirectional connections), how to build real-time (Socket.IO, events, rooms, lifecycle), the hosting challenge (persistent stateful connections don't fit serverless, needing dedicated infrastructure or services), hosted real-time services (the pragmatic way to add real-time without the burden), the collaboration conflict problem and CRDTs (used via libraries, only when truly needed), and why scaling real-time is hard (stateful distributed connections needing coordination, reinforcing the case for services). And this *completes the Real-World Features phase*: payments (W13), email (W14), file handling (W15), and real-time (W16), the capabilities beyond CRUD that turn a working app into a real product. The throughline of the phase is that real products need real infrastructure features, each with its own subtlety and "use the specialist for hard, non-differentiating infrastructure" judgement, and you can now add all of them correctly.

## Where this fits
You shipped a real-time feature with correct real-time architecture, completing the Real-World Features phase (payments, email, files, real-time), the capabilities that turn an app into a product. Next comes the **Performance & DX phase** (W17-20): testing, performance (Web Vitals, bundle size), CI/CD, and observability, the engineering practices and developer experience that make an app fast, reliable, and maintainable, the qualities that separate a working prototype from a production-grade product.

items.body: A user is watching their order on the /orders/:id page. The admin updates the order status to "ready". How does the update reach the user's browser? The admin sends a PATCH /orders/:id request to your server. The server updates the database. Then the server calls io.to(`order:${orderId}`).emit('orderUpdated', { status: 'ready' }). The user's browser, when it loaded the order page, ran socket.join(`order:${orderId}`) (via a socket.emit to the server asking to join that room). The server called socket.join on their behalf. Now when the server emits to that room, the user's browser receives the event and updates the UI without a page reload.

weeks.title: Testing, Unit, Integration, E2E
weeks.context:
Testing is how you change code without being afraid. An untested codebase is one where every change might break something that worked before, and the only way to know is to manually click through every feature after every change. Tests make refactoring possible, make onboarding new developers faster, and make sleeping better.

Three types of tests, from fastest to slowest and from cheapest to most expensive. Unit tests verify a single function in isolation. They mock all dependencies. They run in milliseconds. Write them for pure business logic: price calculations, data transformations, validation functions. Unit tests cannot tell you that the system works end-to-end. Integration tests verify that multiple units work together, your API route calling the database, your authentication middleware rejecting unauthorised requests. They use a real (or in-memory) database. They run in seconds. Write them for your API endpoints. They give the most confidence per test written. End-to-end (E2E) tests run a real browser and simulate user interactions. They test the full stack: frontend, backend, database. They run in minutes. Write them for critical user journeys: sign up, login, place an order, subscribe.

Vitest is the test runner for modern TypeScript projects (faster than Jest, better TypeScript support, same API). Supertest is a library for testing Express HTTP endpoints without starting a real server. Playwright is the standard for E2E browser testing.

Testing culture: tests are not just for finding bugs after the fact. Writing the test first (TDD) forces you to think about the interface before the implementation, it often leads to better-designed functions. At minimum, write tests before you fix bugs (the test proves the bug exists, then the fix makes it pass, and the test ensures the bug never comes back).

This week you write unit tests for the pricing logic in Bean Forge, integration tests for the auth and orders API endpoints using a test database, and E2E tests for the signup and checkout flows using Playwright.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have a function calculateOrderTotal(items, discountCode) that applies a discount if the code is valid. How do you unit test this? You do not need a database or a server, create test cases with plain JavaScript objects. Test the happy path: valid items and a valid discount code returns the correct total. Test edge cases: empty items array returns 0, invalid discount code is ignored (or throws, depending on your design), items with 0 quantity are excluded, negative prices are rejected. Each test creates the input, calls the function, and asserts the output. No mocking required, the function takes plain data in and returns plain data out.

weeks.title: Performance, Web Vitals and Bundle Size
weeks.context:
Performance is user experience. A page that takes 5 seconds to load loses users before they see the product. Core Web Vitals are Google's performance metrics and a ranking signal for search. The three that matter: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), how fast the main content appears; Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), how much the page jumps around while loading; Interaction to Next Paint (INP), how fast the page responds to user interactions.

LCP targets: under 2.5 seconds is good, 2.5-4.0 seconds needs improvement, over 4.0 seconds is poor. The LCP element is usually the hero image or the main heading. Optimise it by: preloading the LCP image (link rel="preload"), serving images in WebP or AVIF format, using a CDN so the image is served from an edge location close to the user, and using the Next.js Image component which does all of this.

Bundle size is the other major performance lever. Every kilobyte of JavaScript downloaded, parsed, and executed delays interactivity. Your users on slow connections pay for every unused import. Measure bundle size with next build (it shows route bundle sizes) and the next-bundle-analyzer package. Common problems: importing an entire utility library when you only need one function (import { format } from 'date-fns' is fine; import _ from 'lodash' pulls in 70KB), not code-splitting large components (dynamic imports load them lazily), shipping polyfills for browsers you do not support.

Server components in Next.js App Router are a performance win: they render on the server and ship zero JavaScript to the browser. Use server components for anything that does not require interactivity (fetching data, static content). Move interactivity down to leaf components that can be marked 'use client'. This "islands architecture" minimises client-side JavaScript.

Caching is the most impactful optimisation. Next.js caches at multiple levels: build-time static generation (fastest), route-level caching with revalidate, and request memoization. Understand which cache is active for each page and when it is invalidated. Database query caching: use Redis or a query-level cache for expensive queries that do not need to be real-time. HTTP caching: set Cache-Control headers correctly so browsers and CDNs cache static assets.
